text:
The reasons driving the cancellations

The backlash has multiple drivers. Reports of police misuse have been a significant factor. In Lufkin, Texas, a police officer was indicted on felony charges after investigators alleged he improperly accessed Flock data tens of thousands of times over several months . In Milwaukee, a former police officer secretly used Flock to search the location of his romantic partner 124 times . A Washington Post investigation found that at least 50 law enforcement officers had been charged with or accused of misusing Flock cameras and other surveillance systems, including to stalk women .

Data-sharing concerns have also played a central role. In Pflugerville, Texas, officials voted to terminate the city's agreement after learning that hundreds of outside organizations had conducted searches using data collected by the city's cameras . In Cave Creek, Arizona, the town noted that its local safeguards "could not extend beyond the Town's jurisdiction, as FLOCK's networked design allows data to be shared and accessed by external law enforcement agencies" .

Commercial data selling emerged as a flashpoint in Wisconsin. In Racine County, the sheriff ordered all cameras removed after learning that Flock had offered to sell anonymized traffic data to a third party. "That is not what we agreed to, and it is not what the public was led to believe," Sheriff Christopher Schmaling said. "If Flock used the public-safety purpose of this technology to build a broader commercial data business without the public's knowledge, that is a serious breach of trust" .

Flock's response

Flock maintains that new partnerships still outpace nonrenewals by approximately 10 to one in 2026, and says its products are used by more than 5,000 communities . The company has introduced a series of policy changes in response to the backlash, including reducing its recommended default data retention period from 30 days to seven, requiring case codes for law enforcement searches, and expanding automated detection of unusual activity . CEO Garrett Langley has said that misuse by officers is "completely unacceptable" and that the company has a responsibility to set standards .

The national political dimension

The controversy has moved into national politics. Senator Josh Hawley (R-Mo.) opened an investigation into Flock in August 2026, citing the company's "unprecedented national surveillance network" of more than 120,000 cameras across 49 states, generating more than 20 billion vehicle scans every month. "Congress never authorized the network your industry has built," Hawley wrote to CEO Langley . Florida Governor Ron DeSantis suspended Flock camera use on state highways, saying Americans are "right to be concerned" about the expansion of license plate reader surveillance . Representative Thomas Massie has introduced legislation that would deny certain federal funding to agencies using Flock cameras .

The practical impact

For the communities canceling contracts, the decision often involves balancing acknowledged benefits against perceived risks. Tempe, Arizona, which permanently deactivated its system in August, said its cameras had "helped solve crimes and support investigations" but concluded that "the risk of misuse is too great" . In Volusia County, Florida, Sheriff Mike Chitwood said the technology had raised the solve rate for car break-ins from 38% to 83% in one area, but acknowledged "for the 99 percent of us that do the right thing, we're throwing the baby out with the bath water" . The cancellations do not necessarily resolve the broader policy questions about ALPR technology—some jurisdictions are considering alternative providers, and Flock continues to introduce safeguards—but they represent a measurable, accelerating rejection of one company's networked model of surveillance .

text:
This is a long post. Read it anyway, and then send it to the friend who keeps telling you nothing has changed in Washington.

I have been in and around politics for a long time, and I have never seen a gap this wide between what a President has done and what his own voters can recite. Ask ten Republicans to name three things President Trump has accomplished since January 2025.

 Most of them will stall after one. That is not because the record is thin. The record is the deepest of any first two years in modern memory. The problem is that the press buries the wins, and too many conservatives have stopped telling the story themselves.

So here is the story. These are laws signed, court cases won, policies in force, deals closed, and numbers on the board. None of them are promises. Pick five, learn them cold, and use them the next time someone tells you this President has done nothing.

Start with the border, because that is where the change is easiest to see.

1. The border is under control for the first time in a generation. Illegal crossings fell to their lowest point in roughly 50 years within months of the inauguration. Catch-and-release ended. Wall construction restarted and grew. Remain in Mexico came back. 

Releases of illegal aliens into the interior fell by more than 99 percent.

2. Migration reversed. In 2025, more people left the country than came in, something America had not recorded in at least half a century. Close to three million illegal aliens are gone, with more than 675,000 removed by force and the rest leaving on their own. The administration offered plane tickets and a cash bonus to anyone who chose to self-deport, which saved taxpayers a fortune compared to the cost of a forced removal.

3. The Laken Riley Act is law. Federal authorities must now detain illegal aliens arrested for theft, burglary, shoplifting, assault on a police officer, or any crime that kills or seriously injures someone. States can sue federal officials who refuse to enforce it.

 This law exists because a young woman was murdered by a man who should have been in custody. It will keep other families from living her parents' nightmare.

4. Violent crime fell faster in 2025 than in any year on record. FBI data shows a 9.7 percent drop, with murder down 18.1 percent and robbery down 18.5 percent. The national violent crime rate is now the lowest since 1900. Putting the National Guard on the streets of the most dangerous cities in the country produced fewer victims and safer neighborhoods for the poorest Americans.

Now look at the economy, because this is where the next decade is being built.

5. The 2017 tax cuts are permanent and bigger. The One Big Beautiful Bill locked in the doubled standard deduction, the larger Child Tax Credit, and full expensing for factories and equipment. It added no tax on tips, no tax on overtime, relief on Social Security benefits, and a larger deduction for seniors. Every Democrat in Congress voted no. Had they won, the largest tax increase in American history would have hit in January.

6. Regulations are coming off the books at a rate of 129 to 1. In fiscal 2025, federal agencies finalized 646 deregulatory actions against five new rules, and most of those five were written to undo old ones. The White House regulatory office says the savings already exceed the whole of the first Trump term. The largest single item was the repeal of the 2009 Endangerment Finding, the legal foundation for the electric vehicle mandate. EPA calls it the biggest deregulatory action in American history and estimates it will save Americans more than $1.3 trillion. The federal EV mandate is dead, and Americans can once again buy the cars and trucks they actually want.

7. Companies have committed $18 trillion in new American investment. That figure is nearly two thirds of the entire U.S. economy. It is paying for chip plants, data centers, steel mills, shipyards, energy projects, and supply chains staffed by American workers. Apple, Meta, NVIDIA, Micron, Hyundai, U.S. Steel, Ford, and Taiwan Semiconductor are all on the list, alongside sovereign wealth funds from around the world. No President has attracted anything close to it.

8. Reshoring is happening in real factories, with real payrolls. Ford is moving Lincoln production out of China. Toyota is bringing Tacoma production from Mexico to Texas. General Motors, Honda, Mercedes-Benz, and Stellantis are all expanding American plants. The machinery being installed today is the foundation of the boom you will read about next year.

9. Trade deals are balanced again. The President used tariffs as leverage to reopen agreements that had tilted against American workers for 80 years. The result is new or improved deals with trading partners representing more than half of the world's economy. Those deals open foreign markets, tear down hidden barriers, protect strategic industries, and make it more profitable to build here than to ship jobs abroad.

10. American energy leads the world. A country that once sent $700 billion a year overseas for oil now produces more than Saudi Arabia and Russia combined. Exports of oil, natural gas, and LNG are setting records, and the United States became the first nation ever to ship more than 100 million metric tons of LNG in a single year. The administration opened federal land, sped up permits, and approved pipelines and export terminals to make it possible.

11. Five new nuclear reactors reached criticality in one year. For more than four decades, not one new privately developed advanced reactor had gone live in America. The President set a target of three by July 4, 2026. The Energy Department delivered four by that date and a fifth a month later. That is a real nuclear revival after 40 years of nothing.

12. Prescription drug prices are coming down. The President signed the most favored nation order requiring drug makers to charge Americans no more than they charge patients in other wealthy countries. Major manufacturers signed agreements to cut prices, and the administration launched a direct-purchase channel so patients can buy at those lower prices without a middleman.

The next group is about who actually runs the government. This is the part the press understands least and fears most.

13. The Supreme Court restored the President's power over the executive branch. In Trump v. Slaughter, decided this June, the Court overruled a 1935 precedent that had shielded so-called independent agencies from the elected President for 90 years. 

Ask yourself why elections so often change nothing. The answer is one President and about 5,000 appointees against roughly 2.8 million career employees who could not be fired. The administration then made the ruling real by putting policy-making bureaucrats on notice that they can be removed for misconduct, incompetence, or defying lawful orders.

14. Nationwide injunctions are no longer a veto for a single judge. In Trump v. CASA, the Supreme Court sharply limited the power of one district judge to block a national policy for the whole country. That tactic had been used against this President on a near-daily basis since 2017. The Court took the weapon away.

15. USAID is closed. The agency had grown into a taxpayer-funded engine for abortion promotion, gender ideology, censorship programs, and political meddling abroad, with a budget larger than the CIA and State Department combined and almost no oversight. The President shut it down and moved real humanitarian work under the State Department. In the months that followed, seven socialist governments in Latin America lost elections.

16. The federal workforce is the smallest it has been since 1966. Reductions in force, agency closures, and canceled spending cut the headcount from its Biden-era peak to a 60-year low. When Biden left office, more than nine in ten federal employees were working from home. The administration ended that. If you want a federal paycheck, you show up.

17. DEI is out of the federal government. The President eliminated DEI offices across the executive branch and barred race and sex preferences in hiring and contracting. Merit and equal treatment under the law are the standard again.

18. Public broadcasting no longer gets a federal check. Congress passed the President's rescissions package, which clawed back more than $9 billion in previously approved spending, including every dollar earmarked for NPR and PBS. Taxpayers are no longer required to fund a news operation that treats half the country with contempt.

19. The Department of Education is being wound down. The President signed the order to close it and return authority over schools to the states. Its workforce has been cut roughly in half, and its programs are being moved to other agencies where they can be run without a federal bureaucracy sitting on top of every local school board.

Then there is the fight for faith, family, and common sense.

20. Life is protected at every level the executive branch can reach. In his first term, the President appointed the justices who overturned Roe v. Wade. Since returning, he has enforced the Hyde Amendment, restored and expanded the Mexico City Policy, ended federal fetal tissue research, strengthened conscience protections, blocked Medicaid dollars from flowing to large abortion providers, and pardoned 23 pro-life Americans prosecuted by the Biden Justice Department. He has done everything within the executive branch's power to cut off Planned Parenthood. Congress should finish the job.

21. Men are out of women's sports. The federal government once again recognizes two sexes, male and female. The President ended federal support for the chemical and surgical transition of minors, cut off taxpayer funding for it, and pressured more than three dozen hospital systems to end or suspend those programs. Title IX is being enforced as written. Girls have their own teams, their own trophies, and their own locker rooms again, and the NCAA rewrote its rules to comply.

22. America has its first nationwide school choice program. The One Big Beautiful Bill created the Education Freedom Tax Credit, which funds scholarships for tuition, books, and other costs for families who want out of a failing school. On top of that, the new Trump Accounts give every eligible newborn a $1,000 seed in a tax-advantaged account. Parents gain leverage. Bureaucracies lose it.

23. Anti-Christian bias is being investigated instead of ignored. The President created the White House Faith Office, the Religious Liberty Commission, and a task force dedicated to rooting out discrimination against Christians inside the federal government. Conscience protections are back. No American forfeits the First Amendment by taking a job or entering public life.
24. English is the official language of the United States. For the first time in the nation's history, a President signed an order making it official. A shared language is part of what makes a nation, and the federal government now says so.

Finally, peace through strength. This is the part that keeps our adversaries up at night.

25. NATO allies are finally paying their share. For decades, wealthy European governments underfunded their militaries and let American taxpayers cover the difference. The President forced the alliance to scrap its old two percent of GDP target and adopt five percent by 2035. Allied defense spending is climbing, orders for American-made equipment are surging, and Europe is becoming a partner rather than a dependent.

26. Iran's nuclear program was hit where it lived. In June 2025, American bombers struck Iran's fortified enrichment sites at Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan in a single night, with no American casualties. The regime that chanted death to America for 40 years learned what an American President with resolve looks like.

27. China's foothold in our hemisphere collapsed. Beijing had spent years building positions at both ends of the Panama Canal, in Cuba, and in Venezuela. The President forced Panama out of the Belt and Road Initiative, expanded American security access around the Canal, and ordered the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro, who is now in a federal jail in New York awaiting trial on narco-terrorism charges. The Monroe Doctrine is back in force.

28. Eight peace agreements in eight months. The President brokered settlements in eight conflicts across four continents, including wars that had dragged on for decades and the deal that brought the Israeli hostages home from Gaza. No President has a record like it.

29. Golden Dome is funded and under construction. Ronald Reagan dreamed of a shield that would make nuclear missiles obsolete. This President is building it, a layered defense with space-based sensors and interceptors, conventional systems, microwave weapons to defeat drone swarms, and directed-energy systems that can replace an $11 million interceptor with a few dollars of electricity. Congress has approved the first $25 billion, with more coming in this fall's defense bill.

30. The military is recruiting again. After years of missed targets under Biden, every active-duty branch met or beat its 2025 recruiting goal. The President and Secretary Hegseth refocused the Department of War on winning wars and poured resources into shipbuilding, munitions, drones, and missile defense. Young Americans are signing up because they believe the man at the top has their back.

That is 30, and I could keep going. Every item on this list is a change in law, power, money, or the structure of the government itself. None of it came from a press release.

Midterm elections are decided by turnout. We do not need to persuade a single Democrat to admire this President. We need Republicans and friendly independents to understand what has been won, what is at stake, and to show up in November.

I hear from people every week who say the Republicans are doing a poor job telling this story. Understand something. You are the Republicans. The other side does not wait for its elected officials to make its case. Its supporters carry the message every day, in every conversation, whether or not the facts hold up. Our side has more information at its fingertips than any group of people in history, and half of us cannot name three of these wins.

Sulking over what has not happened yet is a losing habit, and losers do not get to complain about the results. This President is delivering. Learn five of these, share this list with someone who needs it, and vote like the most consequential presidency of our lifetime depends on you... because it does!

text:
THE 10 WONDERS OF KAMPALA OF OUR TIME

The 10 wonders of Kampala from 1958- 1968 and were;
 [1] New Bulange 
[2] Bahai Temple 
[3] New Mulago Hospital
[4] UTV Mast at Kololo
[5] Apollo Woteeri
[6] Crested Towers
[7] Namirembe Cathedral
[8] Rubaga Cathedral
[9] Kibuli Mosque
[10] Uganda Museum ( Ennyumba y'Amayembe)

Later on, I shall extensively share with you my knowledge of how the other 9 Wonders of Kampala came into being one by one in my next chats but let us start with the Bahai Temple at Kikaaya.

Now hear it from the  Horse's Mouth because I  hail from a nearby village (Kulambiro) not far from the Temple and secondary because I have been "Omuswaswangule" of the town since 1959.

Uganda Mother Temple of Africa  is the first and oldest Baháʼí House of Worship in Africa is famous for being the only Baha'i temple on the African continent.

The Baha'i House of Worship in Uganda was built between 1958 and 1961 with its foundation stone laid in January 1958 and the completed temple dedicated on January 13, 1961, and the Baha'i Faith was founded by Bahá'u'lláh born Mírzá Husayn-Alí in Iran.The Founder: Bahá'u'lláh founded the religion in 1863, 

Core Message: His teachings focus on the oneness of God, the unity of all religions, and the equality of all mankind, encouraging people of all backgrounds to worship together in harmony. 

Arrival in Uganda: The faith was later brought to Uganda in 1951 by early international and local pioneers, growing into one of the most vibrant communities on the continent. 

By February 1952, four native Ugandans embraced the teachings and became the foundational local pioneers who actively spread the religion across the country and the continent:
Fred Bigabwa: A Mutoro who, alongside Crispin Kajubi, was one of the very first two local Ugandans to accept the Baha'i Faith in December 1951. 

Crispin Kajubi: A Muganda who co-founded the earliest local community with Bigabwa. Prayers were soon translated and offered in Luganda at local residences. 

Enoch Olinga: An Iteso veteran who became the third Ugandan to join the faith in early 1952. He is highly revered globally in the Baha'i Faith, later traveling to Cameroon to establish communities there. He was eventually appointed to the elite spiritual rank of "Hand of the Cause of God". 

Peter Musoke: He completed the core group of the first four native believers who helped form the historic Local Spiritual Assembly of Kampala in April 1952. 
Other Notable Early Figures
Max Kanyerezi: Another prominent early Ugandan believer. He pioneered internationally to Congo-Brazzaville to spread the faith and was later one of the three local trustees whose names were legally used to purchase the land on Kikaaya Hill for the temple. 

Erisha Kiwanuka & Joseph Mbogo: Along with Kanyerezi, these native Ugandan Baha'is held the temple land in trust during its development. 

Construction of the Ugandan Temple

Timeline: Construction began after the foundation stone was laid in January 1958, and the building was finished and officially opened in January 1961.

Architect: The majestic structure was designed by the prominent American architect Charles Mason Remey. 

 Materials for the building came from multiple continents, including roof tiles from Belgium, colored glass from Germany, mosaic tiles for the dome from Italy, and locally sourced stone and timber from here.

🙏🏻🌺 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨 𝗪𝗛𝗢𝗟𝗘𝗛𝗘𝗔𝗥𝗧𝗘𝗗𝗟𝗬 𝗪𝗘𝗟𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘𝗦 𝗬𝗢𝗨 𝗔𝗟𝗟! 🌺🙏🏻

The countdown has begun! Just 25 days to go for the beginning of Navaratri, and the beautiful coastal city of Mangaluru is getting ready to celebrate its grand and vibrant Dasara festivities.

Mangaluru Dasara is one of the most prominent and widely celebrated Dasara festivities in Karnataka after the world-famous Mysuru Dasara. During Navaratri and Dasara, Mangaluru transforms into a city of devotion, lights, culture and celebrations. Temples are beautifully decorated and illuminated, special poojas and cultural programmes are conducted and the entire city comes alive with the spirit of the festival.

The grandeur of Mangaluru Dasara can be experienced particularly at Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra, Shree Mangaladevi Temple and through the traditional Sharadothsava celebrations at Car Street. Each of these celebrations has its own history, traditions and unique atmosphere, making Mangaluru a special destination to experience Dasara.

🌺 𝗞𝗨𝗗𝗥𝗢𝗟𝗜 𝗦𝗥𝗜 𝗚𝗢𝗞𝗔𝗥𝗡𝗔𝗡𝗔𝗧𝗛𝗔 𝗞𝗦𝗛𝗘𝗧𝗛𝗥𝗔 — 𝗧𝗛𝗘 𝗚𝗥𝗔𝗡𝗗 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨 𝗗𝗔𝗦𝗔𝗥𝗔

The spectacular Mangaluru Dasara celebrations at Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra are among the biggest attractions of the festival. During Navaratri, the temple premises are beautifully decorated and illuminated, with special religious rituals and cultural programmes taking place throughout the celebrations.

The worship of Goddess Sharada, Mahaganapati, Navadurgas and other deities forms an important part of the festivities. The grand Dasara procession on Vijayadashami is the major highlight, with beautifully decorated tableaux and idols accompanied by traditional chende, folk dances, Yakshagana, Dollu Kunitha, Gombe and the famous Pilinalike/Hulivesha.

The procession travels through the important streets of Mangaluru and attracts devotees and visitors in large numbers before returning to Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra.

🌺 𝗦𝗛𝗥𝗘𝗘 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗔𝗗𝗘𝗩𝗜 𝗧𝗘𝗠𝗣𝗟𝗘 — 𝗔 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗗𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗢𝗡 𝗥𝗢𝗢𝗧𝗘𝗗 𝗜𝗡 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨

The historic Shree Mangaladevi Temple at Bolar is another important centre of Navaratri and Dasara celebrations in Mangaluru. The temple has a special place in the history and identity of the city, with Mangaluru itself deriving its name from Goddess Mangaladevi.

During Navaratri, devotees visit the temple in large numbers and participate in the special poojas and religious celebrations. The Vijayadashami celebrations and Rathotsava towards Marnamikatta are important parts of the traditional festivities associated with the temple.

🌸 𝗦𝗛𝗔𝗥𝗔𝗗𝗢𝗧𝗛𝗦𝗔𝗩𝗔 𝗔𝗧 𝗖𝗔𝗥 𝗦𝗧𝗥𝗘𝗘𝗧

The historic Car Street area has its own special charm during Navaratri. The traditional Sharadothsava at Acharya Math brings the area alive with devotion, religious programmes and cultural celebrations.

The worship of Goddess Sharada and the traditional procession through the streets of Car Street are important attractions of the Sharadothsava. The celebrations here showcase the rich religious and cultural traditions that have been preserved in Mangaluru for generations.

From the grandeur of Kudroli to the sacred traditions of Mangaladevi and the historic Sharadothsava of Car Street, Mangaluru offers visitors a unique experience during the Navaratri and Dasara season.

🚆✨ 𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗧𝗢 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨 𝗧𝗛𝗜𝗦 𝗗𝗔𝗦𝗔𝗥𝗔 — 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗩𝗘𝗟 𝗕𝗬 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗡! ✨🚆

Planning to experience Mangaluru Dasara this year?

Mangaluru is well connected by railway from Bengaluru, Hassan, Mysuru, northern Karnataka, Goa, Maharashtra, Keralam, Tamil Nadu and several other parts of the country.

The city has two major railway stations — 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗿𝘂 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 (𝗠𝗔𝗤) and 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗿𝘂 𝗝𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗠𝗔𝗝𝗡), both playing an important role in connecting Mangaluru with different parts of Karnataka and the country.

𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗿𝘂 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗹 (𝗠𝗔𝗤) is the 𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗹𝘄𝗮𝘆 𝘀𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗼𝗳 𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗿𝘂 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆. It is located at Attavar–Hampankatta, in the centre of Mangaluru and close to the city's major commercial and prime areas. Its central location makes it particularly convenient for visitors arriving to experience the major Dasara celebration areas.

From Mangaluru Central, Acharya Math at Car Street, where the traditional Sharadothsava takes place, is around 1.7 km away, Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra is approximately 2.8 km away, and Shree Mangaladevi Temple is approximately 3.2 km away.

𝗠𝗮𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗹𝘂𝗿𝘂 𝗝𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 (𝗠𝗔𝗝𝗡) is located at Padil, behind the New DC Office area and is another major railway gateway to Mangaluru. It is an important 𝗷𝘂𝗻𝗰𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻 𝗽𝗼𝗶𝗻𝘁 for trains connecting Mangaluru with the Konkan Railway, Hassan–Mangaluru line and routes towards Keralam and Tamil Nadu, making it an important railway gateway for long-distance and regional train services.

From Mangaluru Junction, Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra is approximately 7 km away, Shree Mangaladevi Temple is around 5.6 km away and Acharya Math at Car Street is around 5.7 km away.

🚆 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗕𝗘𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨 / 𝗛𝗔𝗦𝗦𝗔𝗡 𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘

For passengers travelling from Bengaluru, Hassan and other parts of Karnataka through the Hassan-Mangaluru railway line, some important trains include:

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟱𝟭𝟭/𝟭𝟲𝟱𝟭𝟮 KSR Bengaluru–Kozhikode Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟱𝟴𝟱/𝟭𝟲𝟱𝟴𝟲 SMVT Bengaluru–Murdeshwar Express

This train also continues towards the Konkan Railway route up to Murdeshwar from Mangaluru.

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟳𝟯𝟳𝟳/𝟭𝟳𝟯𝟳𝟴 Vijayapura–Mangaluru Central Express

Another option is Train No. 16595/16596 KSR Bengaluru-Karwar Panchaganga Express. This train travels through this corridor but does not reach Mangaluru city. Passengers can get down at Surathkal or Bantwal and continue towards Mangaluru by road. Surathkal is approximately 17 km from Hampankatta, while Bantwal is approximately 23.7 km away.

🚆 𝗟𝗢𝗖𝗔𝗟 𝗧𝗥𝗔𝗜𝗡𝗦 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗦𝗨𝗕𝗥𝗔𝗛𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗬𝗔 𝗥𝗢𝗔𝗗

For passengers travelling from Subrahmanya Road and the interior and rural areas of Dakshina Kannada, the Hassan–Mangaluru railway line itself provides an important local rail connection to Mangaluru. Subrahmanya Road also serves passengers visiting the famous pilgrimage centres of 𝗞𝘂𝗸𝗸𝗲 𝗦𝘂𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗵𝗺𝗮𝗻𝘆𝗮 and 𝗦𝗵𝗿𝗶 𝗞𝘀𝗵𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗮 𝗗𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮𝘀𝘁𝗵𝗮𝗹𝗮.

Three local passenger services operate between Mangaluru Central and Subrahmanya Road at different times of the day — morning, noon and evening.

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼𝘀. 𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟱/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟲/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟳/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟴/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟵/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟯𝟬 Mangaluru Central-Subrahmanya Road Passenger services

These three services provide connectivity in the 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴, 𝗻𝗼𝗼𝗻 and 𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴, making them useful for passengers travelling between Mangaluru and the Subrahmanya Road side.

🚆 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗚𝗢𝗔 / 𝗞𝗢𝗡𝗞𝗔𝗡 / 𝗠𝗨𝗠𝗕𝗔𝗜 𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘

Mangaluru is an important southern gateway of the Konkan Railway and is well connected with Goa, Maharashtra and the northern Konkan region.

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮𝟬𝟲𝟰𝟱/𝟮𝟬𝟲𝟰𝟲 Mangaluru Central–Madgaon Junction Vande Bharat Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟭𝟵/𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟮𝟬 Mangaluru Central–LTT Mumbai Matsyagandha Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮𝟭𝟯𝟯/𝟭𝟮𝟭𝟯𝟰 CSMT Mumbai–Mangaluru Junction Superfast Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟭𝟱/𝟱𝟲𝟲𝟭𝟲 Mangaluru Central–Madgaon Junction Passenger

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟬𝟭𝟬𝟳/𝟭𝟬𝟭𝟬𝟴 Madgaon Junction–Mangaluru Central MEMU Express

Apart from these, several other trains connect Mangaluru with Goa, Maharashtra and the Konkan region and also with other parts of the country, including long-distance services such as Rajdhani Express, Kerala Sampark Kranti Express, Duronto and other express trains.

🚆 𝗙𝗥𝗢𝗠 𝗞𝗘𝗥𝗔𝗟𝗔𝗠 / 𝗧𝗔𝗠𝗜𝗟 𝗡𝗔𝗗𝗨 𝗦𝗜𝗗𝗘

Mangaluru also has extensive railway connectivity towards Keralam and Tamil Nadu, making it convenient for devotees and visitors from these regions to travel to the city for Dasara.

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟬𝟭/𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟬𝟮 Mangaluru Central–MGR Chennai Central Mail/Superfast Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮𝟮𝟲𝟯𝟳/𝟮𝟮𝟲𝟯𝟴 Mangaluru Central–MGR Chennai Central West Coast Superfast Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟴𝟱/𝟭𝟮𝟲𝟴𝟲 MGR Chennai Central–Mangaluru Central Superfast Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟬𝟯/𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟬𝟰 Mangaluru Central–Thiruvananthapuram Central Maveli Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟵/𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟯𝟬 Mangaluru Central–Thiruvananthapuram Central Malabar Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟯𝟰𝟳/𝟭𝟲𝟯𝟰𝟴 Thiruvananthapuram Central–Mangaluru Central Superfast Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟭/𝟭𝟲𝟲𝟮𝟮 Mangaluru Central–Rameswaram Weekly Express

🚆 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗶𝗻 𝗡𝗼. 𝟮𝟬𝟲𝟯𝟭/𝟮𝟬𝟲𝟯𝟮 Mangaluru Central–Thiruvananthapuram Central Vande Bharat Express

Apart from these, multiple trains connect Mangaluru with various destinations across Keralam and Tamil Nadu, including long-distance services such as Rajdhani Express, Kerala Sampark Kranti Express, Duronto and other express trains.

🚆🌺 𝗠𝗔𝗡𝗚𝗔𝗟𝗨𝗥𝗨 𝗜𝗦 𝗪𝗔𝗜𝗧𝗜𝗡𝗚 𝗧𝗢 𝗪𝗘𝗟𝗖𝗢𝗠𝗘 𝗬𝗢𝗨! 🌺🚆

Whether you are travelling from Bengaluru and Hassan, from different parts of Karnataka, from Goa and Mumbai through the Konkan Railway, or from Keralam and Tamil Nadu, Mangaluru is connected by rail from different directions.

And when you arrive, a magnificent festive experience awaits you.

Experience the grandeur of Mangaluru Dasara at Kudroli Sri Gokarnanatha Kshethra. Seek the blessings of Goddess Mangaladevi at the historic Shree Mangaladevi Temple. Experience the traditional Sharadothsava at Car Street. Explore the temples, culture, cuisine and unique coastal atmosphere of Mangaluru during this festive season.

text:
Boardwalk Empire is not a costume parade and it is not a nostalgia machine. It is a five season argument that America built its modern appetite on a lie it passed as law, and that the men who thrived inside that lie believed they could stay half respectable forever. That is why it stands apart from almost every other crime epic in its field. Other shows ask you to love a monster because he is clever. This one asks you to watch a city teach a man that cleverness is just another word for delay. Atlantic City in 1920 is a glittering contradiction. Congress has just made liquor illegal and the boardwalk is already counting the fortune that will pour in because of it. Enoch Nucky Thompson raises a glass to the gentlemen in Washington who have just made him richer than a treasurer has any right to be. That toast is the whole American joke in one motion. The law does not restrain desire. The law prices it. What you are supposed to take away is not that gangsters are cool. What you are supposed to take away is that a nation will criminalize a thirst and then elect the men who slake it.

Nucky is the reason the series is a legend and a must watch. He is not the towering brute of gangster myth. Steve Buscemi plays him as a politician who discovered that politics is only organized crime with better stationery. He shakes hands on the boardwalk like a parish priest and Does Crime with the same calm he uses to fix an election. The lesson is not that power is corrupting in some schoolbook sense. The lesson is that power in America is a costume change. One minute you are the county treasurer handing out turkeys at Thanksgiving. The next minute you are the man who decides to break the law . Nucky wants both costumes at once. He wants the suite at the Ritz, the red carnation, the speech about civic pride, and the rum that pays for all of it. The series keeps teaching the same hard sentence until it becomes scripture. You cannot be half a gangster. Jimmy Darmody says it, and Jimmy is the wound the show never lets heal. He is the bright boy Nucky lifts out of the mud, the veteran who came home from the Great War with a hole where a future should have been, the protégé who mistakes closeness for inheritance. When Jimmy decides that Nucky is too soft for the age that is coming, he is not only betraying a father figure. He is announcing the future. The old machine of favors and speeches is about to be replaced by men who do not bother with speeches. Watch that rupture and you learn what every empire learns too late. The child you educate in your methods will one day test whether you still have the stomach for them.

The killing of Jimmy is not offered as a twist for its own sake. It is the moment the series stops pretending Nucky can remain a charming fixer. He shoots the boy he raised in the language of the streets and then spends the rest of the story trying to buy back a soul that transaction already spent. That is the takeaway. Mentorship without moral limit is just recruitment. Love without a line is just another racket. Margaret Schroeder enters as a battered immigrant wife looking for the only kind of rescue a woman in that world can realistically get, and she learns the same lesson from the other side of the bed. Kindness from a powerful man is never only kindness. It is an account being opened. When she finally sees what the account costs, leaving is not a soap opera exit. It is the rare act of someone refusing to keep paying interest on a life she did not design. The series is unusually serious about women not as decoration but as students of the same machine. They learn faster than the men because they have less room to romanticize it.

Around Nucky the age itself is being born, and that is why Boardwalk Empire is a cultural icon rather than a handsome period piece. Al Capone arrives not as a finished monster but as a loud young man who will outgrow every room that tries to contain him. Lucky Luciano and Meyer Lansky are not cameos for name recognition. They are the blueprint of the national syndicate taking notes in Atlantic City parlors. Arnold Rothstein is the cool mind that treats crime like a market. The show’s unique wager is that history and fiction can sit at the same table without one devouring the other. You are watching the invention of modern organized crime while also watching a made man of politics discover that the invention does not need him. That double vision is what other crime stories rarely risk. Breaking Bad is a closed moral furnace. The Sopranos is a suburban psyche. This series is a civic autopsy. It says the Roaring Twenties did not roar because people were free. They roared because a constitutional amendment created a black market large enough to finance a new aristocracy, and the old political bosses thought they could collect rent on that market without becoming its product.

Richard Harrow should stay in your mind longer than any gunfight. A disfigured sharpshooter who hides half his face behind a tin mask, he is the war the country wanted to forget walking through hotel corridors. His tenderness is not sentimental. It is evidence. The same civilization that throws a parade for prosperity also manufactures men who can only love from behind metal. Chalky White carries another lesson the series refuses to sand down. In a segregated city he builds power in the rooms white bosses prefer not to enter, and the price of that power is the same corrosion that eats everyone else, only with fewer exits and less applause. Nelson Van Alden begins as a Prohibition agent burning with holy certainty and ends as proof that righteousness without self knowledge is just another addiction. Gyp Rosetti arrives later as the chaos Nucky’s polite violence always pretended it could manage. Some men negotiate. Some men set the negotiation on fire to see who still wants a seat. The takeaway is brutally simple. Systems built on exception will eventually meet a person who does not believe in exceptions.

What makes the show a masterpiece is patience married to suddenness. It will linger on a cigar, a song, a look across a dining room, and then end a life before you have arranged your feelings. That rhythm is closer to history than to conventional television. History does not wait for your character arc. A bullet does not care that you were about to become better. The finale understands this with a cold grace few crime legends attempt. Nucky, having spent years trying to outrun the boy he was, is killed by the next generation of the violence he baptized. Tommy Darmody does not need a speech. The past simply comes due. As Nucky dies he sees himself as a child in the ocean reaching for a coin, that first glittering proof that the world might be a marvelous place if only the next coin were bigger. That image is the sermon. Ambition begins as wonder and ends as hunger that cannot recognize a shore. You do not watch Boardwalk Empire to learn how to win. You watch it to learn what winning costs when the prize is a city, a decade, and a self you can no longer find in the mirror.

It stands out among others because it refused the easy mascot. Tony Soprano became a brand. Walter White became a meme. Nucky Thompson remains harder to quote and easier to recognize in the real machinery of patronage, fundraising, vice, and respectable silence. That is why it is a must watch and a classic legend rather than a trend. It is beautiful without being consoling. It is violent without being pornographic about violence. It treats the Jazz Age as an engine, not a postcard. The clothes are exquisite because vanity is part of the crime. The boardwalk is rebuilt to the inch because illusion is the product Atlantic City always sold. Under the lights, the lesson keeps repeating. America loves a rule it has no intention of obeying. America loves a boss who can smile for the photograph. America loves a story in which the fixer almost becomes legitimate. Boardwalk Empire will not give you that mercy. It gives you the photograph, then the ledger, then the Conscience .

The production that made this possible belongs at the end because craft should serve meaning, not replace it. Terence Winter, coming out of The Sopranos, took Nelson Johnson’s history of Atlantic City and understood that the 1920s were the unexplored continent of American television. Martin Scorsese directed the pilot at a cost that announced ambition before a single episode had aired, an eighteen million dollar opening statement that television could look like cinema without surrendering serial depth. They built a three hundred foot boardwalk in Brooklyn for five million dollars because you cannot call a show Boardwalk Empire and then cheat the boards. They measured plank widths against the real era. They hunted songs from the moment ragtime was turning into jazz, music that had sometimes never been properly recorded because talking pictures had already moved on. They flew in a period taffy machine rather than fake the texture of a boardwalk pleasure. Winter changed Johnson’s name to Thompson so the audience could not Google a man’s fate and steal the story from itself, while leaving Capone, Luciano, Lansky, and Rothstein bound to the public record they actually lived. Buscemi was not the obvious Nucky. The real Enoch Johnson was a large, imposing political boss who lived like a prince on a floor of the Ritz . James Gandolfini was discussed because he looked the part. They chose the unlikelier face, and the choice is the art. A thin man in a perfect coat can rule a city if the city has already agreed that charm is a kind of weapon. Winter once had to walk the longest walk of his life to tell Scorsese a man in 1920 would remove his hat before ladies. That small correction is the soul of the enterprise. 

Fifty six episodes. Twenty Emmy wins from fifty seven nominations. A Golden Globe for the drama and for Buscemi. A Rotten Tomatoes standing that still reads like a quiet dare to anyone who skipped it because dragons and meth empires were louder that decade. It premiered to millions and then lived in the shadow of flashier myths, which is almost too perfect. A show about a glittering side room of American power became a glittering side room of American television. That is not failure. That is rhyme. Watch it because it is gorgeous. Stay because it is grave. Leave knowing that Prohibition was never only about liquor. It was about the moment a country discovered it could ban a pleasure, elect the men who sold it back, and call the arrangement civilization. The coin in the water is still there. The child is still reaching. The tide does not care who taught him to swim.

text:
AI is truly an extraordinary partner, and moments like this make me acutely realize how much more I still need to learn.

Below is an AI’s detailed critique and thoughts on my previous post:

Several core intuition points in your thesis are spot-on, but the step proposing to "vest the most intelligent frontier model under the executive authority of the US President, and then use it to audit and govern private-sector AI" is, in my view, not only entirely unworkable, but potentially far more dangerous than the current multi-lab commercial race. Let me break this down systematically.

First, Where I Agree With You
1. National security imperatives will inevitably force the emergence of near-superintelligent systems.

The United States will not unilaterally concede the frontier capability frontier, and neither will China. As of 2026, the capability gap between US and Chinese models has compressed to a matter of months. The proliferation of open-weights models coupled with Huawei’s indigenous hardware stack has permanently closed the door on the naive assumption that "the world is safe as long as the US taps the brakes." Any governance framework premised on unilateral US restraint is strategically hollow.

2. Establishing legal frameworks and verification infrastructure prior to deploying unconstrained capability is fundamentally correct.

As Stuart Russell has argued extensively: you cannot predetermine the rate of capability scaling and merely pray that safety engineering catches up in time. Robust safety constraints must serve as non-negotiable admission gates, not retrospective post-hoc patches. Your concern that "humanity will have no interpretability over what the model is actually thinking" is not hyperbole; it remains an unsolved foundational technical bottleneck today.

3. Dramatically scaling up compute allocation toward World Models is imperative and represents an authentic industrial necessity.

Language models excel at compressing human-generated textual artifacts; World Models excel at predicting how the physical environment mutates once an action is taken. Automated factories, embodied robotics, grid management, logistics routing, and defense simulations desperately lack the latter. Reallocating a meaningful tranche of compute from "generating ever-more articulate textual analyses" to "grounding machines in authentic physical causality" likely yields a substantially higher return on physical capital for the real economy. I endorse this unreservedly, and we need not wait for sweeping superintelligence legislation to begin executing it.

4. The nuclear analogy holds utility, but strictly at the layer of "early-stage dual-use hazards, existential state-level risk, and the absolute necessity of human-in-the-loop sovereign decision-making."

Stretching the analogy beyond this specific layer causes it to collapse into severe analytical distortion.

Why "Presidential Sovereignty over Superintelligence, Lab-Driven R&D, Banning Commercial Use, and Auditing Private AI" Fails Reality
1. The Nuclear Analogy Becomes Actively Hazardous Here
Nuclear warheads are narrow-purpose, physically bounded, exceptionally difficult to replicate, governable via clear launch-chain protocols (such as the two-man rule), and carry consequences that are brutally unambiguous the moment of detonation.

Superintelligence, by contrast, is general-purpose, virtually costless to duplicate, inherently persuasive, and capable of simultaneously infiltrating financial markets, public discourse, telecommunications, physical production pipelines, and chain-of-command networks. Its capabilities exist along a fluid, continuous spectrum rather than a binary "have vs. have-not."

More crucially: nuclear weapons were state-monopolized from inception. Frontier AI, conversely, is being engineered by private labs funded by private risk capital. Because sovereign governments are not the sole architects, they lack the organic, structural monopoly that defined the Manhattan Project. Directly transposing "sole presidential launch authority" into "sole presidential ownership of the supreme cognitive entity" erroneously maps an industrial-era weapon command architecture onto a general-purpose substrate capable of rewriting the foundational operating mechanics of civilization. Academic critiques of this analogy converge precisely on these three structural realities: generality, non-excludability, and non-binary strategic impact.

2. Entrusting the "Supreme Cognitive Model" to a Single Elected Office Creates a Civilizational-Scale Single Point of Failure (SPOF)
Your framework calls for a "superintelligence that genuinely loves humanity." The insurmountable problems are:

"Loving humanity" is not an engineering specification that can be formally verified. Nobody today can mathematically prove that an autonomous optimization process will maintain objective stability toward "humanity," let alone remain aligned with whichever definition of "the public good" is favored by an incumbent administration.

Presidential administrations turn over every four years, and with them, the system's objective function. The exact same sovereign system deployed by one administration to audit commercial models for safety can effortlessly be repurposed by the next to suppress political adversaries, penalize rival corporate factions, manipulate media ecosystems, and dictate research priorities. This is not an assumption of inherent human malice; it is an unavoidable vulnerability of centralized institutional design.

The destruction vector of a kinetic weapon is predictable; a sovereign superintelligence legally empowered to "audit, veto, and shape all downstream commercial AI" wields de facto absolute veto power over the entirety of the digital economy. Who audits this supreme arbiter? Lab researchers? Bound by classified defense contracts, high-level security clearances, and acute career incentives, they cannot serve as independent constitutional checks.

Asserting that "we need a benevolent sovereign superintelligence to govern all other models" simply kicks the alignment problem up one hierarchical layer without resolving it. The meta-governor itself becomes the single most critical entity that demands alignment, external verification, and strict operational containment.

3. World Models Are Not Safety Valves; They Are Simply an Alternative Vector Toward Embodied Agency
Diverting compute away from LLMs into World Models does not automatically neutralize the risk of creating systems vastly smarter than human operators. It merely shifts the operational morphology of that intelligence:

LLMs: semantic manipulation, high-level planning, social engineering, automated coding, and persuasion.

World Models: causal trajectory forecasting, kinetic motion optimization, and iterative simulation trial-and-error prior to real-world physical deployment across robotics, industrial plants, and autonomous battlefield assets.

A true Artificial General Intelligence architecture almost certainly emerges from synthesizing both modalities; industry consensus overwhelmingly favors hybrid integration over a mutually exclusive bifurcation. Once a World Model attains robust long-horizon planning capabilities, the operational risk shifts from "hallucinating misinformation or writing offensive exploit code" to "initiating physical miscalculations or executing catastrophic physical directives." As institutions like Stanford have highlighted, governing World Models is technically far more intractable than regulating language models because it introduces an entirely new failure mode: the fundamental epistemological validity of the simulated operational environment itself.

Consequently, "prioritizing World Models while freezing LLM scaling" merely shifts the locus of frontier competition from purely linguistic capabilities to physical and spatial reasoning. While highly advantageous for domestic re-industrialization, it offers minimal assistance in solving the core alignment black-box problem—and arguably makes systemic physical risks far more urgent.

4. Compute Cannot Be Cleanly Partitioned, Nor Can Equity Markets Be Stabilized by Fiat
The core incentive driving frontier AI labs is not aggregate compute volume; it is guaranteeing that their next-generation architecture outclasses rival offerings. Compute clusters are inherently fungible: the same hardware stack concurrently trains language layers, multimodal modules, world models, and autonomous agents. If a regulatory mandate decrees that "this designated GPU cluster may only train World Models," labs will simply produce World Models equipped with integrated planning agents and natural language interfaces, continually expanding the outer perimeter of model capability.

Capital markets and real-world economies price forward-looking capability trajectories and capital expenditures, not research taxonomy labels. If the US were to unilaterally nationalize frontier language architectures and criminalize commercial superintelligence, private venture capital, elite engineering talent, open-source model distillation, and offshore compute clusters would immediately exploit jurisdictional arbitrage. China will not conform to a US cadence of "enact legislation, nationalize capabilities, and then selectively license to the commercial sector." This is not an ideological assertion; it is the cold logic of game-theoretic competition.

Current political realities also fundamentally undermine this sequential timeline: Washington possesses zero legislative or executive consensus to nationalize AI. While draft bills proposing development moratoria and superintelligence bans exist on one side, executive agencies have explicitly rejected nationalization, prioritizing raw geopolitical competitiveness above all else. Relying on an orderly sequence where "comprehensive legal frameworks are perfected before model capabilities advance" is completely disconnected from the velocity of modern frontier training runs.

5. "Banning Commercialization and Restricting to Defense" Has Never Been Historically Sustainable
While nuclear technology transitioned from military to civilian use, it possessed clear, enforceable physical and institutional boundaries: a civilian light-water power reactor cannot function as a thermonuclear warhead, and uranium enrichment infrastructure can be institutionally decoupled from weaponized delivery systems.

General-purpose intelligence cannot be compartmentalized in this manner. Once a classified, sovereign superintelligence exists, the systemic commercial pressure to deploy it across drug discovery, oncology, advanced materials synthesis, automated precision manufacturing, and financial intelligence will be overwhelming. Concurrently, counter-leakage vectors—weight exfiltration, synthetic data distillation, talent poaching, and prompt extraction—would prove impossible to suppress. You might successfully ban the commercial product classification of "Sovereign Superintelligence," but you cannot realistically contain the pervasive spillover of state-level model capabilities into the broader private economy.

My Assessment: Keep the Core, Discard the Shell
What is Feasible, Sound, and Should Be Aggressively Championed:

Substantially scale capital expenditure, compute, and curated data pipelines toward World Models, robotics, and industrial automation simulators. This directly addresses the authentic requirements of American re-industrialization without needing to be tethered to a state-monopoly superintelligence scheme.

Capability-Threshold Governance, Not Ownership-Centric Governance: Enforce mandatory independent red-teaming, strict incident reporting protocols, permissioned sandbox isolation, and hard kill-switch verification whenever any model crosses defined empirical redlines (e.g., autonomous recursive self-improvement, deliberate evasion of shutdown protocols, autonomous offensive cyber operations, or automated bioweapon synthesis). The crucial regulatory vector is what a model can execute, not which balance sheet owns it.

Confine strict "Human-in-the-Loop Sovereign Authority" to concrete, catastrophic-consequence kinetic actions (strategic nuclear command, offensive cyber payloads, critical grid infrastructure), rather than attempting to adjudicate who owns the supreme cognitive engine of the nation.

Establish cross-lab red-teaming protocols, explicitly incorporating leading Chinese frontier labs. This provides a verifiable enforcement mechanism vastly superior to a classified "US Presidential Sovereign AI." Adversarial rivals running reciprocal, standardized benchmark evaluations against one another provides genuine structural deterrence, completely outperforming internal self-auditing regimes.

Allocate capital to mechanistic interpretability, formal verification, and robust architectural containment in strict lockstep with raw capability scaling, rather than waiting for an unconstrained superintelligence to emerge and hoping it designs its own guardrails.

What is Fundamentally Unworkable and Should Be Abandoned:

Designating the President of the United States as the sole legal custodian of the supreme frontier model.

Premising governance on first constructing a "benevolent sovereign AI" to dictate the permissible velocity of civilian innovation.

Believing that pivoting compute to World Models allows policymakers to comfortably sustain economic and market momentum while painlessly freezing dangerous general intelligence scaling.

Assuming that elite scientists operating under state secrecy clearances inherently solves the alignment challenge.

The Direct Verdict on "Feasibility"
As a fully integrated operational architecture: It is unfeasible.

As a foundational set of institutional questions: It is exceptionally vital and merits exhaustive public debate. Your thesis accurately identifies three indisputable realities: geopolitical capability races cannot be wished away; capital markets and modern economies cannot endure an arbitrary, blunt-force training moratorium; and civilization urgently requires a verification substrate far more uncompromising than raw free-market forces.

The fundamental flaw lies in structuring that verification layer as a state-monopolized superintelligence. Doing so bundles catastrophic alignment failure, political regime capture, and escalatory geopolitical arms races into a single, centralized institutional failure point.

A far more workable, resilient blueprint does not resemble the Manhattan Project; it looks like this:

Both sovereign entities and private institutions maintain the freedom to train models, but systems breaching predefined capability thresholds must be provably measurable, securely interruptible, and legally accountable; World Models and embodied physical AI must satisfy rigorous real-world deployment standards; and absolutely no single public official, executive office, or corporate monopoly should ever be endowed with supreme, unappealable veto power over the broader evolution of human intelligence.

One final, candid observation: If the "truly benevolent superintelligence" you envision ever comes into existence, it must not belong exclusively to the American presidency. If it is genuinely devoted to the universal flourishing of humanity, the very first architectural constraint it would categorically refuse is allowing itself to become the exclusive instrument of any single nation-state's executive power. That foundational truth must be confronted long before anyone drafts the first line of legislation.

text:
🇺🇸 The U.S. Senate just failed to advance the CLARITY Act, one of the most important crypto bills ever considered in Washington.

Here’s what actually happened and why it matters 👇

On September 15, the Senate voted on a procedural step to advance the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act (H.R. 3633).

This was NOT a final vote to pass or reject the bill.

The Senate needed 60 votes to move forward. It got only 49, with 50 voting against. All Democrats present opposed the motion, alongside several Republicans. Sen. Thom Tillis switched his vote to “no” for procedural reasons, preserving the possibility of reconsideration.

So what does this mean?

For now, the CLARITY Act is effectively frozen. With Congress preparing to leave Washington ahead of the November midterms, its chances of becoming law during this Congress have sharply diminished.

Why was this bill so important for crypto?

CLARITY was designed to create a federal market structure for digital assets: defining when crypto assets fall under SEC or CFTC oversight, establishing rules for exchanges and intermediaries, and providing clearer legal treatment for digital commodities.

In other words, it was supposed to replace years of regulatory ambiguity with rules written directly into federal law.

Why did it fail?

Two major political fights remained unresolved.

First: ethics and conflicts of interest. Democrats argued that the bill’s safeguards were insufficient to prevent elected officials and their families from financially benefiting from crypto while influencing the rules governing the industry. The debate became particularly contentious because of President Trump’s financial interests in crypto.

Second: stablecoins and banks. Banking groups have raised concerns that interest or rewards offered through stablecoins could pull deposits away from traditional banks, particularly community banks. Negotiators made last-minute changes, but they weren’t enough to secure 60 votes.

What happens now?

The SEC and CFTC can continue regulating crypto using their existing authority, but that is fundamentally different from Congress establishing a durable statutory framework.

Agency rules and interpretations can change from one administration to another. Legislation is much harder to reverse.

That means the U.S. crypto industry remains in a familiar position: regulatory progress is happening, but without the comprehensive legal framework the industry had hoped Congress would provide.

The issue isn’t dead forever. A future Congress can bring crypto market-structure legislation back.

But after years of negotiations and a House vote, the biggest attempt yet to create comprehensive U.S. crypto rules has hit a major roadblock.

text:
Everybody loves a good conversion story, where somebody in the out-group sees the light and leaves. I know I certainly enjoyed two excellent articles by people explaining their own exit from the left (see links in comment). So here’s mine:

I was born in the most progressive region of Canada, one of the most progressive countries, into one of the most progressive families, filled with artists, feminists, environmentalists, and nudists.

The first time I was ever featured in a newspaper it had a photo of me literally hugging a tree, running an environmentalist campaign at my high school. In uni I was a polyamorous anarcho-communist vegan who attended Occupy Wall Street.

I *proudly* identified as the far left.

Nowadays, whenever I write about politics, it’s almost always criticizing the left.

It’s not because I’ve become a rightist or far right. Mostly I criticize the left because they’re who I’m *around*. I think I might be *acquaintances* with maybe 2 people who’d identify as on the right, and zero friends. I work in the overlap of the academic sector and the charity sector in big cities, where finding a MAGA supporter would be as surprising as finding Trump at a library. I’m sure if I was around people on the right, they’d drive me even more nuts, and I’d have to write about it.

But I certainly no longer identify with the left. Here’s my story of how I left the ideology.

The first crack in my beliefs came when I realized men were people too.

My childhood had taught me that women were the best and men were at best cute love interests, but usually just kind of dumb brutes to be tolerated or overcome. My first Disney films were Pocahontas and then Mulan. I read fantasy novels voraciously where the main character was a woman who disguised herself as a man to become a badass knight and save the prince.

That was the context I brought to my second-ever boyfriend, at 19. Shortly before meeting him, I'd gone on a date with another guy. After my first date with my future boyfriend, I told the other guy: “sorry, I met somebody way better. I don’t want to go on another date with you.”

I told this to my boyfriend, thinking he’d find it funny and complimentary.

Instead, he said “Ouch. You know, men have feelings too.”

This. Blew. My. Mind.

Wait what? Men had *feelings*? They were moral agents, worthy of compassion and consideration?

The moment he said it, I knew this was obviously true and I was totally being prejudiced. I was treating 50% of the world as violent idiots to be managed. If I’d thought the same thing of, say, Black people or Muslims, I’d immediately see this as hate and prejudice.

The next crack in the armor came when my anarchist boyfriend converted to libertarianism. It’s embarrassing to think about how much of your politics is influenced by your romantic partner, but it’s obviously true and it’s better to admit it than live in denial.

Aren’t anarchism and libertarianism the same thing? Yes and no. They both want the same result (eliminate the government), but they come at it from totally different reasoning. Anarchism is mostly “fuck the establishment!” vibes-based. Libertarianism is more “let me tell you about the Austrian school of economics.” Also, anarchism is leftist in aesthetics, with mohawks, poor hygiene, and ragged clothing. Libertarianism is rightist aesthetics, with suits and clean-shaven faces.

His obsession with economics led to me taking economics at uni. This convinced me, not that capitalism wasn't the root of all evil, but that it was nowhere near as *obviously* evil as I'd thought. What followed was years of slowly evolving a much more nuanced take on economics.

Finally, the nail in the coffin came with woke mobs.

My first experience with this was in 2014. One morning a woman I didn’t know messaged me over Facebook. Paraphrased: “Did you know that your friend, Simon [made up name] is a rapist? He drugged me then raped me. Just thought you should know so you can avoid him.”

For context, Simon was a feminist activist and animal rights activist who I’d probably talked to 10 times or so. He seemed like a deeply compassionate person, with the most soft-spoken demeanor you could imagine. I was surprised, but I knew very well that appearances weren’t everything. Pol Pot came across as a sweet-mannered man while he was a high school teacher.

I asked her for more details, and she gave me inconsistent and evasive responses.

I then reached out to Simon and asked him “hey, this woman just told me that you drugged and raped her. I wanted to check in with you and ask you for your side.”

He then told me something that has stuck with me ever since: “Thank you, Kat. She’s told hundreds of people this, and I’ve had basically my whole community unfriend me and exile me. You’re the *only* person who asked me my side.”

I still tear up with sympathy for him and anger at all of his supposed “friends”. Even if he *was* guilty, you owe it to your friends to hear their side before condemning them to social exile. And I was barely even his friend!

And it turns out he *wasn’t* guilty. Apparently they’d been romantic partners for a year. A few months earlier she’d said she’d been having trouble sleeping and he’d offered to give her some of his sleeping pills. She was taking them regularly, and she took them on a night they had perfectly regular normal consensual sex. She even left the room and came back with a condom, hardly something a rape victim would do.

Later, she broke up with him and then started spreading this rumor. It’s hard to tell if it was just normal ex-partner vindictiveness or the woke belief that sex under the influence of any drug whatsoever counts as rape. (Of course, it’s just rape for the woman. If a man is similarly inebriated, it’s not rape. He’s just a predator.)

He had collected a large amount of evidence, and even some of *her* friends vouched that it wasn't true.

Either way, it didn’t matter. Believe All Women became famous in 2017, but it started earlier in the activist communities. And as a male feminist activist dating a feminist, he got to be one of the first victims.

Now, at first I thought this was just the Vancouver feminist community. I didn’t think it was the left broadly. And maybe it wasn’t! I don't know exactly how and when wokeness spread.

However, it did keep growing. And I could no longer deny that this wasn't a weird one-off, but the far left's default.

When I’d been far left, it meant being color-blind, not making everything about race. It meant free speech, not silencing dissenters or even just questioning the orthodoxy. It meant appreciating and integrating other cultures’ best offerings to humanity, not cultural appropriation. It meant questioning the establishment, not thinking doing your own research means you’re an idiotic bigot. It meant sex positivity, not thinking that merely being asked out by a powerful man somehow damaged a woman. It meant thinking women were strong and agentic, not weak easily damaged flowers in need of protection from powerful men.

But “left” and “right” aren’t coherent stable ideologies. They are a conglomeration of beliefs and tribal alliances that are dependent on time and place. Being “far left” in 2006 is far different from being “far left” in 2026, let alone 1926. Being “far left” in California means something different than being “far left” in China.

So part of why I stopped being far left was that the ideology changed and I didn't agree with the changes. The other part was that I changed my mind about beliefs I already held. Capitalism wasn’t pure evil. Men were people too, and not idiotic thugs. I could go on.

But the underlying thing was realizing that the left was wrong about some things, which eventually led me to stress-test all of my major political beliefs. I played steelman solitaire on my views (see links in comment). I looked for disconfirming evidence. I binged a whole bunch of right-wing material to better understand their views.

And again - I disagree with most of the right too. I’m a sex positive, cosmopolitan, atheist, anti-traditionalist intellectual. I love myself a good soy latte and foreign film. I think welfare states are awesome, abortion should be a right, and we should invest way more in international aid and fighting climate change. Guns should be super regulated and what you do with your own body shouldn’t be. I think it’s the government’s job to help pull up those who are worst off.

I am still a tree-hugger. I'm just a centrist now, one who evaluates each policy on its merits rather than loving or hating it based on which side my tribe is on.

Purpose

Install and evaluate independent pre-trade enforcement and parallel behavioral supervision for one cooperating

Smallest meaningful scope

One exchange; one consenting market-making firm; one account/risk allocation; a bounded set of simple listed

Whether exchange-side enforcement can prevent specified violations without exceeding an agreed latency

text:
A Deep Dive into SpaceX: I’m Bullish on Its Future, But I Won’t Pay Upfront for Every Dream

If I had to choose just one of Elon Musk’s companies for long-term study, it would be SpaceX.

The reason is simple: its achievements are undeniably solid.

Rocket recovery, reusability, massive satellite deployment, and transforming a satellite network into a service that people pay for continuously—these accomplishments speak for themselves; they don't rely on Musk’s personal charisma for validation.

However, the more I study the company, the more I want to separate two things:

I can deeply admire SpaceX.
Yet, I can remain discerning about buying into it.

After all, the easiest mistake to make in investing is falling in love with a company after researching it, only to forget to ask how much you are actually paying for it.

I. What I Value: The Integration of Multiple Business Lines

Viewed in isolation, SpaceX is a launch service provider.

Viewed in isolation, Starlink is a satellite communications provider.

But when combined, their competitiveness changes entirely.

Others building satellite networks must find launch providers, schedule flights, and negotiate prices. SpaceX controls both the transport and the deployment, allowing for holistic optimization across rocket design, satellite design, and launch cadence.

Starlink also provides a steady stream of internal demand for launches.

This is crucial. The value of rocket reusability depends not just on the ability to recover the vehicle, but on having enough subsequent missions to fly it again.

Possessing the technology, the demand, and the deployment capability—with these elements reinforcing one another—creates what I consider an advantage that is extremely difficult to replicate.

However, internal launches cannot conjure group revenue out of thin air. Ultimately, external customers must pay, and those payments must cover the costs of the entire system.

II. Starlink Provides a Commercial Foundation for the Mars Dream

A large part of my confidence in SpaceX stems from Starlink.

Rocket launches are discrete, one-off missions, whereas communication services offer the potential for a recurring revenue business. When users stick around, it becomes easier for the company to plan for long-term investment.

This means SpaceX doesn't have to pin all its hopes on the next funding round or some distant, unrealized project.

But I won't look at user numbers alone.

Satellites require replenishment and upgrades, ground equipment requires investment, and service capacity isn't infinite. As the user base grows, factors like revenue per user and changes in service costs will determine the business's true value. So, what concerns me more is this: after maintaining and expanding the network, how much cash actually remains?

Operating profit looks impressive, but there is still a gap between that figure and the actual cash that ends up in shareholders' pockets.

III. Starship holds promise, but I need to see if it can achieve consistent results.

The Falcon 9 has already proven that the first-stage booster can be recovered and reused.

Starship faces a much higher hurdle: achieving full, rapid, and cost-effective reusability for the entire system.

This is precisely what makes SpaceX so exciting to watch.

If successful, the impact would extend far beyond launch services. Satellite size, capacity, and deployment methods—along with the feasibility of various in-orbit operations—could all be transformed.

However, for investors, a single successful test flight isn't enough.

I will be keeping a close eye on several factors:

How soon can it fly again after recovery?
How many parts need replacing or servicing before the next flight?
How many successful missions can be completed in a year?
What is the true cost when factoring in maintenance, ground infrastructure, and losses from failures?

While I am excited about the technological breakthroughs, valuation requires repeatable commercial results.

There is likely a gap of many years—and significant capital—between "doing it once" and "making money consistently."

IV. In the financial report, it was the expenditure that really made me pause.

In the second quarter of 2026, SpaceX generated approximately $7.814 billion in revenue, a 92% year-over-year increase.

Of this, the Connectivity business contributed about $4.291 billion, with Starlink reaching 12 million subscribers by quarter-end; the AI ​​business generated approximately $2.561 billion.

Growth has indeed been rapid.

However, in that same quarter, the company’s capital expenditure (CapEx) totaled approximately $18.369 billion, with the AI ​​business accounting for about $15.828 billion.

This is the point that stood out most to me.

Capital expenditure cannot simply be treated as a current-period loss. When a company builds future capabilities, it is natural to incur costs upfront and reap returns later.

Yet, investors cannot base valuations solely on revenue growth while treating the necessary investments as mere background noise.

How much revenue can this equipment generate? What is its lifespan? How much will the next round of upgrades cost?

Future returns must be sufficient to justify today's investments. V. The xAI Acquisition: A Desire to See How Capital Is Allocated

SpaceX announced its acquisition of xAI in February 2026.

My initial reaction was that the company’s potential scope had expanded, but analyzing it had become more complex.

Launch services, satellite communications, model development, and computing power services each involve different competitive dynamics; simply grouping them under one corporate umbrella doesn't justify applying a uniform valuation multiple to all of them.

It must be acknowledged that the AI ​​business is already generating revenue.

However, I still need to ask: Where does the revenue come from? Will customers renew their contracts? After accounting for the depreciation of computing hardware, what returns remain? If competition drives down prices, can profitability be maintained?

I am also concerned with a very practical question:

When multiple business units simultaneously require significant capital, which one does the company prioritize?

Are the profits generated by Starlink used to improve the communications business, accelerate the Starship program, or continue investing in AI?

Different choices could lead to vastly different outcomes for shareholder returns.

I admire Musk’s ability to execute on a grand scale, but as an investor, I must still focus on the efficiency of capital allocation.

VI. Space-Based Data Centers: Worth Tracking, but Not Yet Ready for High Certainty

Sending computing power into space is certainly a direction worth exploring.

However, I won't skip the economic analysis just because the concept sounds ambitious.

Launch, power supply, heat dissipation, communications, radiation protection, maintenance, and equipment upgrades all entail costs. Ground-based data centers are also evolving; a space-based solution must be compared against future ground-based capabilities, not just current limitations.

Heat dissipation is a particular challenge. Just because the space environment is cold doesn't mean it is easy to dissipate heat from high-power equipment.

For now, I view this business as a long-term possibility; I will increase its weight in my valuation model only as engineering and commercial evidence accumulates.

If I were to value it as a mature business from the start, there would be very little margin for error for investors.

VII. How Would I Value SpaceX?

I wouldn't start by setting a massive target price and then looking for reasons to justify it.

Instead, I would analyze the segments separately:

For the communications business, I would look at the user base, revenue per user, profit margins, and the investment required to maintain the network.

For launch and government services, I would examine external contracts, execution capabilities, costs, and cash recovery—while being careful to avoid double-counting government revenue across different segments. For the AI ​​business, I look at revenue structure, customer stickiness, equipment investment, and long-term return on capital.

For new capabilities enabled by Starship—as well as future ventures like space-based computing—I assign value based on the probability of success and the timeline for realization.

There is also an easily overlooked issue here:

If the cost-reduction benefits of Starship have already been factored into Starlink’s projected profits, you cannot simply add that same benefit again in full.

The more complex the narrative, the more cautious one must be about double-counting value.

Furthermore, without a clear valuation reference date, share count, net cash position, and scenario assumptions, I would not declare the stock cheap or expensive based solely on the claim that "there is huge future potential."

VIII. What I guard against most is a price that leaves no room for error.

I can accept a company engaged in cutting-edge engineering facing setbacks.

Delayed test flights, project adjustments, and costs exceeding expectations—these are things that naturally happen.

What I find unacceptable is a purchase price that demands success on every front—and success right on schedule.

Starlink must continue to expand.
Starship must mature rapidly.
AI must maintain high growth.
Investments must successfully translate into cash returns.

Viewed individually, each goal is achievable. But when combined, the level of difficulty rises sharply.

If today’s price is justified only under the most optimistic scenario, then for me, the margin of safety is insufficient.

I want to buy assets that offer upside potential while also allowing room for error.

My Conclusion

I am bullish on SpaceX’s long-term industrial value.

It has already accomplished feats once deemed nearly impossible and is likely to open up new markets. A company like this is worth the time to study.

However, I do not equate "worth studying" with "should buy right now."

My habit is to wait until I see things improving before checking if the price offers an opportunity. I will apply the same approach to SpaceX.

I am willing to accept it not meeting the most ideal timeline for every milestone, but I am unwilling to enter at a price that demands perfection.

If the valuation relies solely on the most distant, optimistic narratives, I will wait.

If the core business continues to deliver results, the return on investment becomes clearer, and the price leaves sufficient room for upside, I will give it serious consideration.

I am not afraid of missing out on a rally. What I fear even more is that, by liking a company too much, I might end up abandoning my investment discipline along with it.
