text:
🚩India’s middle‑class crisis: the great bifurcation and the Gen Z uprising

(This article states that India's middle class is in crisis ,not experiencing linear growth, as was imagined in the 2000s, but rather significant polarisation: while the elite is prospering, the lower middle class is becoming increasingly vulnerable. Social mobility – which was based on the three pillars of education, jobs in the service sector (particularly in IT), and urbanisation – is functioning less effectively than before. This situation is particularly problematic in a country where, every year, more than ten million young people enter the job market: it is from among them, and from Gen Z at large, that today’s street protesters are drawn )

The student protests we have been witnessing in India can be explained in large part by the crisis facing the Indian middle class, marked in particular by graduate unemployment and a decline in average purchasing power. This is because the upper middle class has grown wealthier, while the lower-middle class has become poorer.

Until the mid-2010s, the idea that India’s middle class was destined to expand continuously seemed self-evident. India had enjoyed double-digit growth during the decade from 2004 to 2014 under Prime Minister Manmohan Singh, the architect of the economic liberalisation of the 1990s driven by the IT sector and foreign investment. The middle class was expanding at that time thanks to the growth of new skilled jobs. This momentum led to the emergence of a social group comprising corporate executives, engineers, IT professionals and entrepreneurs. This middle class defined itself by its income, its consumption capacity, and a social ethos often associated with the higher castes – particularly evident in its opposition to affirmative action policies.

However, this category has remained difficult to measure, as the criteria used vary widely among organisations: income, consumption, wealth, educational level, type of housing, white-collar employment, or subjective self-identification. In the 2010s, several estimates fuelled the notion of a spectacular rise of the Indian middle class. In 2012, the NCAER estimated that it comprised approximately 142 million people, or nearly 12% of the population. Other researchers, using broader criteria, estimated it at 20% of the population. On this basis, firms such as Ernst & Young, McKinsey, and Goldman Sachs predicted rapid growth in this segment, with some even forecasting several hundred million members by 2025–2040.

Narendra Modi, when he was chief minister of Gujarat and later as prime minister after 2014, even used the term “neo-middle class” to refer to people from rural areas who were entering a form of urban modernity thanks to economic growth. However, this term quickly disappeared from political vocabulary as the momentum for expansion ran out of steam.

Indeed, the Indian middle class plateaued in the mid-2010s. According to the Pew Research Center, in 2017, only 108 million Indians belonged to the middle class – defined as having an income of $10 to $50 per day in purchasing power parity – representing about 8% of the population. When the wealthiest segments – those situated above this group – are included, the proportion remains close to previous estimates, confirming the lack of significant growth of the Indian middle class. This is because real incomes for this social category stagnated between 2013 and 2014 and 2023 and 2024. Real wages even declined in several sectors: manufacturing, mining, energy, and services.

This situation can be explained by persistent inflation, particularly food inflation and by weak income growth. Between 2017 and 2018 and 2022 and 2023, real urban income showed virtually no growth. In certain sectors, such as IT, retail, and logistics, nominal wage increases fell short of inflation.

The social implications of a K-shaped recovery

These averages mask a growing internal differentiation within the middle class. Some households formerly classified in this category have joined the economic elite, while the majority of the middle segments have stagnated or regressed. Data from the World Inequality Lab indeed show a dramatic concentration of income at the top of society: the richest 10% held 57.7% of national income in 2022–2023, compared to 33.5% in 1990. The richest 1% held 22.6% of national income, and the top 0.1% held about 10%. India now has more than 300 billionaires. Conversely, the 40% below the top 10% saw their share of national income drop from 44.1% in 1990 to 27.3% in 2022–2023, while the share of the poorest 50% fell to 15%. This situation has led some researchers, such as Lucas Chancel and Thomas Piketty, to speak of a “missing middle class.”

This polarisation is reflected in consumption patterns. The poorest half of the urban population spends less than 5,000 rupees per month, while the richest 5% spend more than four times as much. Households drew heavily on their savings after the pandemic, but this was not enough: their debt has reached a record high, while demand for consumer goods is slowing. Car sales are telling, as only 12% of Indians are reportedly able to afford a car. Small cars, previously associated with the middle class, are declining, while SUVs and high-end vehicles are growing strongly, as are luxury housing, high-end hotel services, and business-class airline tickets.

This polarisation seems paradoxical in light of India’s officially reported growth rates, which have often hovered around 7 to 8 percent since 2014, excluding the Covid years. How can this paradox be explained? First, these figures have been disputed, particularly due to issues with national accounting and the overestimation of the informal sector. The IMF itself has criticised the quality of India’s data. In reality, growth is believed to have been overestimated by 1.5 to 2 percentage points. This is because several shocks have hit the economy hard: the 2016 demonetisation, which abruptly removed 85% of the currency in circulation and had a lasting impact on the informal economy; the poorly managed introduction of the Goods and Services Tax in 2017, which disrupted small and medium-sized enterprises; and then the Covid-19 pandemic, which caused a collapse in economic activity, a massive exodus of precarious workers, and a major social crisis.

Second, since the pandemic, India’s recovery has been described as “K-shaped” growth: the wealthiest are benefiting from growth, while the working and middle classes are stagnating or declining. In 2024, three quarters of Indians earned less than 15,000 rupees per month – about 140 euros. This unequal recovery explains why macroeconomic growth is not translating into an expansion of the middle class. It primarily benefits an elite capable of investing, consuming high-end goods, and capitalising on the opportunities of globalisation, while college graduates face a deteriorating job market.

Graduate unemployment and turbulence in the IT Sector

Young Indians with higher education face very high unemployment rates. In 2024, according to the International Labor Organization, the unemployment rate among graduates reached 29.1 percent – nine times higher than that of illiterate people. This new paradox stems in part from a mismatch between graduates’ expectations and employers’ needs – both in terms of quality and quantity. Families invest heavily in private education, often at the cost of significant debt, which leads young people to turn down low-paying jobs. At the same time, employers believe that many graduates lack the necessary skills. Top-tier institutions, such as the Indian Institutes of Technology, remain highly selective and train only a small minority of engineers. And even these institutions are facing placement difficulties, with a significant drop in job offers in 2023–2024.

The IT sector, long a driving force behind the rise of the middle class, illustrates this crisis. The growth of India’s IT sector was fuelled by outsourcing from the West – particularly in the wake of the Y2K bug – by the training of qualified engineers, and by supportive public policies, such as the creation of special economic zones. Companies such as Tata Consultancy Services, Infosys, Wipro, and Satyam-Mahindra have made India a global powerhouse in IT services. The sector accounted for 7.4% of GDP in 2022, up from 1.2% in 1998, and its exports exceeded $200 billion in the mid-2020s, with the United States absorbing a dominant share of these exports.

But India’s IT sector is slowing down. Revenue growth has levelled off, investments have declined, and the workforce is no longer expanding. Automation and artificial intelligence threaten a significant portion of jobs. Major companies in the sector have begun to reduce their workforces: Infosys, Wipro, and TCS have laid off employees or scaled back hiring. The Indian IT sector could benefit from the rise of Global Capability Centers, or GCCs. These centers are established directly in India by foreign multinationals to bring certain IT, financial, HR, or innovation functions in-house. By 2025, India had approximately 1,700 GCCs employing 1.9 million people, with an annual growth rate of 19%. They could expand further due to the cost of skilled labour and visa restrictions in the United States. However, these centers do not recruit large numbers of recent generalist graduates; they primarily seek specialised, experienced professionals with advanced skills in AI, cybersecurity, or cutting-edge technologies. This trend is therefore likely to exacerbate polarisation in the labour market rather than help expand India’s middle class.

Overall, the middle class is not experiencing linear growth, as was imagined in the 2000s, but rather significant polarisation: while the elite is prospering, the lower middle class is becoming increasingly vulnerable. Social mobility – which was based on the three pillars of education, jobs in the service sector (particularly in IT), and urbanisation – is functioning less effectively than before. This situation is particularly problematic in a country where, every year, more than ten million young people enter the job market: it is from among them, and from Gen Z at large, that today’s street protesters are drawn.

Christophe Jaffrelot is the author of Modi’s India (Princeton University Press, 2021. His next book L’ambition indienne : les paradoxes d’une nouvelle puissance (éditions Taillandier) is due to be released in October 2026.

text:
THE HIDDEN SPIRITUAL DANGER OF SEX, HUGGING, & KISSING.

MEN, READ THIS CAREFULLY.

There are exchanges that the body calls pleasure and the world calls love. The unseen calls them something else.
Every touch is a current. Every kiss is a door. Every union is a merging of fields.

When two bodies press together, it is not only skin that meets. Auras interpenetrate. Subtle cords form. Vital essence — the same force the ancients named jing, ojas, prana, or inner fire — is offered, taken, or scattered. What feels like closeness can become a silent hemorrhage of the soul’s reserve.

Hugging is not always innocent. Prolonged embrace without inner stillness allows another’s unresolved grief, hunger, or restlessness to enter your field. You walk away carrying a weight that is not yours. The heart feels heavier and you cannot name why.

Kissing is a more intimate breach. Breath mixes. The mouth is a gate of spirit. In that moment two nervous systems, two emotional histories, two unfinished destinies briefly occupy the same current. If the other is uncentered, fragmented, or carrying heavy karmic residue, that residue does not stay on their side of the kiss.

Sexual union is the deepest of these rites. It is not merely physical. It is a temporary fusion of two entire energetic bodies. Soul-ties are not poetry; they are residual threads that continue to pull long after the bodies have parted. Pleasure can mask the cost: scattered life-force, weakened will, a subtle dimming of inner light, and an increased openness to influences that do not serve the soul’s ascent.

This is not a condemnation of intimacy. It is a warning about unconscious intimacy. The danger is not the act itself. The danger is the absence of sovereignty while the act occurs.

A man who has not gathered himself — who has not learned to contain his own fire, to stand inside his own field, to remain the still point even in closeness — leaks. He becomes a vessel others drink from without knowing they drink. He gives away the very substance needed for vision, endurance, and inner kingship.

The mystics of many lineages spoke of this. They did not speak from fear of the body. They spoke from knowledge of the subtle body. Conservation is not repression. It is the refusal to let the sacred current be spent on what does not nourish the deeper life.

Before you open, ask:
•  Is this exchange feeding the flame or feeding the shadow?
•  Will I walk away more myself, or less?
•  Is there presence here, or only hunger wearing the mask of affection?

The body will always want contact. The soul wants contact that does not cost its light.

Guard the gates. Not with hardness. With awareness.
The most dangerous thing is not the kiss.
It is kissing while asleep.

Wake up first. Then decide what you allow through the door.

text:
THE UNDERLYING LOGIC

The agreement responds to a concrete problem: the Iran war has depleted US stocks of precision-guided missiles and air defense interceptors, while demand from European allies and Ukraine continues to rise . Pistorius framed Germany’s offer plainly: “We offer know-how and capacity for joint production. We fill our own stocks, we strengthen our capabilities, and we also strengthen those of our partners” . He noted that “if US capacities are not sufficient—and given the large demand figures, that is definitely the case in some areas—we have offered to produce in Germany. That is meeting with a lot of goodwill” . The agreement also aligns the US Department of Defense’s acquisition transformation strategy with Germany’s Procurement Acceleration Act .

GERMANY’S NEW POSITION

Hegseth credited Germany with approaching fulfillment of NATO’s 5% defense spending commitment made at the Hague Summit, calling it “leading the way” . He added that “defense spending is only the first step. A NATO 3.0 also requires that Germany’s very large and tradition-rich industrial base be used for common defense” . Pistorius said Germany supports greater European responsibility for conventional defense: “We Europeans want to take some of the burden off the US and assume primary responsibility for conventional deterrence in Europe” . Germany currently hosts about 38,000 US soldiers, making it the most important US base in Europe .

WHAT IS NOT SETTLED

The praise did not resolve all open questions. Pistorius confirmed that details on the Tomahawk cruise missile delivery to Germany still need to be clarified, and that delivery timelines are uncertain because the US is consuming its own stocks in the Iran conflict . On the US troop presence in Europe, Pistorius said both sides want to prevent “dangerous capability gaps” and confirmed that the US review of its deployment posture should be completed by the end of the year . The Pentagon had announced the withdrawal of 5,000 US soldiers from Germany in the spring, and Pistorius said there was no criticism from Hegseth “regarding overflight rights or other matters” related to the Iran war . The trip continues with Pistorius traveling to New York for talks at the UN and then to Fort Worth, Texas, where he will receive the first of 35 F-35A fighter jets ordered for the German Air Force .

text:
Omnia Buy Adds to Solar Inds' Explosive Growth, But Valuations High

The Deal
Solar Industries India signed a definitive deal to acquire 100% of South Africa's Omnia Holdings through its wholly owned step-down subsidiary Solar SA Investments Proprietary Limited

All-cash deal worth $1.35 billion (₹12,950 crore) — to be concluded by mid-2027

Omnia had a turnover of $1.41 billion in FY26 — valuation multiple is around 16 times Omnia's FY26 profits of ₹800 crore

What Omnia Brings
Diversified global company headquartered in Johannesburg — chemical businesses with exposure across mining, agriculture and chemicals

Operates across 23 countries with presence in key mining regions across Africa, Australia, South America and agriculture markets in Australia, Brazil and the USA

Mining division (BME brand): leading provider of mining solutions including blasting systems, explosives, mining chemicals and metallurgical processing — operates across South Africa, broader SADC region, Indonesia, Canada, Australia and the USA; produces bulk explosive emulsions, packaged explosives, non-electric and electronic detonators and blast-design software; strong R&D profile

Chemicals segment: manufactures and distributes specialty chemicals and solutions to South African and export markets — bulk trade, water care, disinfectants and filtration products

Agriculture business: produces and trades granular, liquid and specialty fertilisers, humates and biostimulants; offers agronomic advisory services

Strategic Fit for Solar Industries
Omnia amongst the largest players in Africa — offers a global platform for commercial explosives and blasting solutions — "a clear fit"

Omnia mining business has synergies with Solar's existing South Africa operations

Gives Solar enhanced market share in Australia and Indonesia and helps it enter new markets — Canada and Brazil

Mitigates supply risk; creates flexible supply chain with increased capacity for ammonium nitrate storage and production and access to phosphates

May accelerate Solar's next growth phase — creating a large, integrated explosives and blasting solutions platform with global scale

Solar Industries — Business Profile
India's largest integrated explosives and energetics firm — market leader in industrial explosives and defence products

Has leveraged expertise in mining explosives and initiating systems (detonators) into becoming a defence manufacturer — producing ammunition, propellants, warheads, Pinaka rockets, loitering munitions and high-energy materials

FY26 inflection point: consolidated revenue grew 30% YoY — robust growth in defence (27% revenue contribution), global businesses (39%) and others (34%)

Entered FY27 with order book of ₹21,300 crore — multi-year revenue visibility

Management (pre-acquisition) guided FY27 revenue of ₹14,000 crore — implying 40% YoY growth while maintaining steady Ebitda margins

Defence Segment — Driving Quality
Defence grew 93%, exports by 32%, others by 3% in recent period

Higher deliveries of rockets, ammunition, propellants, warheads, high-energy materials and loitering munitions

Order pipeline driven by high-value defence programmes including Pinaka rocket systems, ammunition, propellants and warheads

Company transitioning from industrial explosives manufacturer dependent on mining cycle into a technology-driven defence manufacturing platform

Valuation — High But Backed by Growth
Two-year forward P/E has historically been in the 60 times range — current prices around 55 times expected FY28 EPS

Revenue, EBITDA and PAT all expected to register annual growth rates of mid-30s or better through FY28

Average one-year analyst target price: ₹24,292 — stock slumped 13.7% to close at ₹19,250 on BSE on Tuesday

Six of seven Bloomberg analysts are "bullish"; one is "neutral"

Key Risks
Sharp increases in raw material and energy costs could hurt margins — though management says it can negotiate contractual pass-through mechanisms

Delays in contract execution could also impact revenue

Valuations consistently high as investors have bet on the growth story

text:
🇮🇳🇷🇺 Russia's BMP-3 Push Puts India's Own FICV Programme in the Crosshairs — Again
WHAT: Russia is actively pushing India to acquire the upgraded BMP-3 infantry fighting vehicle — featuring modular reactive armour (4S24 Kaktus), anti-cumulative grilles, and self-sealing fuel tanks — to replace India's aging BMP-1/BMP-2 fleet.
WHEN: Offer first surfaced October 2025; brought back into active discussion during the Indian Army Chief's Russia visit roughly 2 weeks ago (early September 2026), alongside spare parts and air defence talks.
WHO: Russia (via Rostec/High Precision Systems), pitching to the Indian Army — this isn't the first attempt; India rejected an earlier BMP-3 offer back in 2013 to protect its own FICV ambitions.
WHY: India's BMP-2 fleet — several hundred vehicles built under licence since the late 1970s — forms the backbone of the Mechanised Infantry but is increasingly outdated against modern battlefield threats. Russia frames BMP-3 as informed by real combat lessons from Ukraine.
THE INDIGENOUS PROGRAMMES AT STAKE:
🔹 FICV (Futuristic Infantry Combat Vehicle): India's own ~$10 billion, 2,600-vehicle indigenous programme has been stuck in delays for over a decade. A BMP-3 purchase — even as a "stopgap" — has historically threatened to sideline FICV entirely; that's exactly why India said no in 2013.
🔹 Indigenous BMP-2 upgrade programme: The Army is separately pursuing a domestic modernisation path for its existing BMP-2 fleet — this competes directly with BMP-3 as an alternative near-term solution, without needing to introduce an entirely new imported platform and its associated logistics/spares tail.
🔹 Private-sector ICV/IFV efforts: Programmes like NAMICA (tank destroyer) and the Abhay AIFV technology demonstrator have struggled with technical challenges and service rejections — but a Russian import "solving" the capability gap removes the pressure and funding urgency needed to push these indigenous efforts to maturity.
WHY IT MATTERS: This is the same pattern we've flagged before — Javelin vs MPATGM, Thales rockets vs the IIT Madras/BEL system. A "faster, proven" import consistently competes with slower, harder-fought indigenous development at exactly the moment domestic programmes need sustained backing to cross the finish line. If India takes the BMP-3 route again, it risks repeating a cycle where every capability gap gets patched with an import instead of the pressure being applied to actually fix FICV's decade-long delays. The real question isn't whether BMP-3 is capable — it clearly is — it's whether accepting it removes the last real incentive for India's mechanised infantry modernisation to ever go indigenous.
🇮🇳 Aatmanirbharta doesn't get tested when things are easy. It gets tested exactly in moments like this.

🚨 TRUMP MADE A DEAL WITH ZELENSKY. THEN RUSSIA TOOK THE LAND. NOW TRUMP IS TALKING TO MOSCOW.

The US-Ukraine minerals deal was signed in April 2025. It gave Washington access to Ukraine's rare earths, lithium, titanium, oil, and gas. There was just one problem: 70% of those resources sit in territory controlled by Russia.

➡️ THE DEAL THAT WASN'T — April 30, 2025: the "Reconstruction Investment Fund" is signed. 50% of new extraction revenues go to a joint fund. Ukraine keeps legal ownership. The US gets privileged access. But no security guarantees were included. Forbes Ukraine values Ukraine's mineral wealth at $14.8 trillion. The catch: over 70% is in Donetsk and Luhansk. In other words: the deal was signed for resources Ukraine does not control.

➡️ THE RUSSIAN COUNTER-OFFER — Kirill Dmitriev, head of Russia's sovereign wealth fund, met Steve Witkoff at least nine times since April 2025. The "Dmitriev Package" offers Washington access to Arctic oil and gas, rare earths, nuclear-powered data centers, and a Bering Strait tunnel. The price tag? $12 to $14 trillion. Zelensky called it out first. Dmitriev then raised the figure. Putin's message to Trump is simple: "Russia has resources. America needs resources. Let's make a deal."

➡️ THE DONBASS LEASE — The plan negotiated in Miami between Witkoff and Dmitriev has 28 points. The core: Ukraine leases the Donbass to Russia. Moscow keeps de facto control. Kyiv keeps legal title. A rent is paid. Why lease? Because the Ukrainian constitution requires a referendum to cede territory — and that referendum would never pass. The lease is a legal workaround.

➡️ THE STRATEGIC PARADOX — The lease implicitly recognizes that the Donbass belongs to Ukraine — a direct contradiction of Russia's own constitution, which annexed the region in 2022. Moscow is now negotiating from a position of strength because it physically holds what the US-Ukraine deal promised to deliver.

➡️ THE BIG LOSER: EUROPE — Europe is not at the table. It lost cheap Russian gas. It is paying for Ukraine's reconstruction. And it risks being locked out of the rare earth scramble entirely. Emmanuel Todd said it in March 2025: "Europe is afraid of peace." Because peace would force European elites to confront the problems they have ignored for decades.

Trump signed a deal with Kyiv for resources that Moscow controls. Now he's negotiating with Moscow. Ukraine risks being sidelined in a deal about its own soil. And Europe — once again — pays the bill without a seat at the table.

THE FUTURE OF THE WEB: CRYPTOGRAPHY, BLOCKCHAIN, AND THE QUANTUM QUESTION
A Case Study on the Internet Computer Protocol

INTRODUCTION

The modern web stack — a patchwork of centralized cloud providers, password-based
authentication, and legally fragile jurisdictional promises — is under mounting pressure
from three directions at once: rising cyberattacks, geopolitical fights over data
sovereignty, and the looming, still-uncertain timeline of quantum computing. This paper
surveys who is actually pushing the boundaries of applied cryptography and blockchain
architecture, with a deep focus on one project making an unusually broad bet: the
Internet Computer Protocol (ICP), built by the DFINITY Foundation.

PART 1: WHO IS PUSHING THE ENVELOPE

Zero-knowledge proofs remain the most active frontier in applied cryptography. Eli
Ben-Sasson, co-founder of StarkWare, has been researching cryptographic and
zero-knowledge proofs of computational integrity since earning his PhD in theoretical
computer science from Hebrew University in 2001, and is a co-inventor of the ZK-STARK
protocol, the FRI protocol, and the Zerocash protocol. His work exemplifies a shift in
how ZKPs are used — not just for privacy, but for scalability and integrity guarantees
across systems too large to inspect directly.

Institutionally, the Stanford Center for Blockchain Research co-organizes an annual
academic conference on the science of blockchain, and IBM Research is actively
publishing on post-quantum non-interactive key exchange, homomorphic encryption, and
new signature schemes. This is a maturing academic field, not a fringe pursuit.

Against this backdrop, DFINITY's Internet Computer Protocol stands out for the sheer
breadth of what it is attempting: not a single cryptographic innovation, but a full
replacement stack for cloud computing, identity, and application architecture, unified
under one cryptographic protocol. With over $500 million invested in research and
development, DFINITY's team — composed of engineers and researchers formerly from
Google, Apple, IBM, and Meta — has published more than 1,500 papers, earned 88,000+
citations, and contributed 190+ patents across distributed systems, cryptography, and
advanced computing. Few blockchain projects can point to that volume of peer-reviewed
output, which meaningfully separates ICP from projects whose claims rest primarily on
whitepapers and marketing.

PART 2: A DIFFERENT WEB STACK

ICP's core technical wager is chain-key cryptography: threshold cryptographic schemes
that let a network of independent nodes collectively sign and authenticate without any
single node — or small colluding subset — ever holding the full private key. Chain-key
cryptography enables subnets of the Internet Computer to jointly hold cryptographic
keys, in a way that no small subset of potentially misbehaving nodes on the subnet can
perform useful operations with the key, but the majority of honest nodes together can.
This has enabled smart contracts hosted on the Internet Computer to directly interact
with other blockchains, without needing dangerous centrally-controlled bridges or
wrapping — a meaningful advantage given how frequently cross-chain bridges have been
hacked across the industry.

Architecturally, ICP departs from the conventional three-tier web stack (frontend,
backend server, separate database). Its fundamental unit is the canister: a
WebAssembly module instance, typically written in Motoko or Rust, that bundles compute
and state together. Variables declared in a persistent actor survive canister upgrades
automatically — there is no database layer, no serialization code, and no pre- or
post-upgrade hooks needed for most use cases. This "orthogonal persistence" removes an
entire category of bugs and complexity that plagues conventional web development,
independent of any blockchain considerations.

Sovereign "cloud engines" extend this architecture further, allowing an operator to
choose the underlying hardware, who operates it, where it is located — for example to
address GDPR or sovereignty concerns — and the replication level for security and
performance. This is not a separate product bolted onto the network; cloud engines are
simply sovereign subnets, scaling through the same horizontal subnet-creation mechanism
the rest of the network uses.

Underpinning all of this is Internet Identity, ICP's passwordless authentication
system. Users can connect passkeys to their Internet Identity and use the secure chip
inside their devices for authentication instead of passwords or clunky two-factor
methods, with sessions further secured by a combination of WebAuthn and threshold
signing. This directly targets the single largest real-world attack vector in modern
breaches: credential and identity compromise, which drives the majority of cloud
security incidents today.

PART 3: THE SOVEREIGNTY AND SECURITY BACKDROP

ICP's pitch has been sharpened by real geopolitical events. The US CLOUD Act, enacted
in 2018, forces US-based tech companies to comply with law enforcement requests for
data even if the information is stored abroad — meaning physical data residency in
Europe no longer guarantees legal protection. In response, France has ordered every
ministry, covering 2.5 million civil servants, to migrate away from Microsoft
dependency, and multiple German states have mandated migration away from Microsoft 365
in government offices. Notably, even hyperscaler "sovereign cloud" offerings have not
fully solved this: AWS's European Sovereign Cloud entity, for instance, remains a
subsidiary of https://t.co/9NKfHDjwir, Inc., a US corporation, meaning jurisdiction still ultimately
follows corporate control rather than physical location.

Europe's actual, present-day answer to this problem — initiatives like the
German-backed Sovereign Cloud Stack, built on open-source components such as
Kubernetes and OpenStack — is winning the adoption race today. It is deployed, today,
across hundreds of thousands of government workstations in Germany, France, and the
wider EU, and worldwide sovereign cloud spending is forecast to reach $80 billion in
2026 alone. ICP, by contrast, remains comparatively small: daily active addresses sit
at roughly 4,600, with total value locked far below Ethereum or Solana.

However, the open-source sovereign stacks and ICP solve different problems. Federated,
open-source stacks primarily address jurisdictional and legal control — who owns and
operates the infrastructure. They do not, by themselves, change the underlying
architecture of centralized data storage. This distinction became concrete in
September 2026, when an identity verification company, IDScan, was breached — hackers
reportedly had a live feed of every ID the company scanned for over a year, ultimately
exposing more than 150 million driver's licenses, 10 million ID cards, and 3 million
travel documents. This was not a jurisdictional failure; it was an architectural one —
a single centralized party holding a massive database of sensitive documents. Open,
federated cloud stacks do not inherently prevent this pattern; they simply change who
legally controls the honeypot. ICP's Internet Identity model, which never centralizes
raw identity documents in the first place, is a structurally different answer to this
specific failure mode.

This pattern extends to breach statistics generally: cloud compromise is often an
identity event first and an infrastructure event second — compromised credentials,
excessive permissions, and misconfigurations turning a single account into broad
access. Forty-five percent of all data breaches now occur in cloud environments, and
cloud-focused attacks are increasing roughly 13 percent annually. A cryptographically
sovereign architecture does not eliminate this risk, but a passwordless, non-custodial
identity model addresses its single largest root cause more directly than jurisdictional
control alone.

PART 4: THE QUANTUM QUESTION

Quantum computing poses a distinct, additional threat: a sufficiently powerful quantum
computer could use Shor's algorithm to break the elliptic-curve and RSA-based
cryptography underlying nearly all of today's digital signatures, including those
securing the web (TLS/HTTPS) and virtually every blockchain in production.

The conventional web is migrating, but unevenly and incompletely. A 2026 measurement of
domains found that roughly half to two-thirds now support hybrid post-quantum key
exchange — the mechanism that prevents "harvest now, decrypt later" attacks on data in
transit. But authentication has lagged badly: zero percent of measured domains have
adopted hybrid post-quantum certificates, leaving the layer that verifies identity
online fully exposed to future quantum attacks. Most large enterprises remain in early
discovery or planning phases of migration. The structural reason is coordination
failure: post-quantum algorithms have existed and been standardized by NIST for years,
but migrating requires millions of independent websites, certificate authorities, and
hardware vendors to each act on their own timeline.

Blockchains face an analogous — and frequently overstated — version of this problem.
Many projects market themselves as "quantum-ready" or "quantum-resistant," but the
claim usually applies to a narrow slice of the system: the signature scheme securing
token transfers, and nothing else. Since Ethereum and similar blockchains are not
quantum-resistant, no token built on top of them is either — token-level security is
entirely inherited from the base chain's signature scheme. Even on chains that have
built genuine post-quantum tooling, adoption can be negligible: Solana's Winternitz
Vault has provided quantum-resistant key rotation for over two years, yet adoption
remains limited to fewer than 300 accounts on mainnet as of April 2026, while the
overwhelming majority of Solana's transaction signing still relies on quantum-vulnerable
cryptography. Industry analysts explicitly warn buyers to watch for red flags:
vague claims about adopting NIST standards "later," optional wallet-level tools
presented as protocol-level security, and projects using quantum fear to drive token
demand rather than shipping real protection.

Crucially, even a genuinely quantum-secured token ledger does not extend that
protection to anything built on top of it. A chain that only secures wallet ownership
and transaction signatures leaves smart contract logic, application data, and identity
systems layered on top entirely outside that protection, because quantum resistance
was never designed to cover them. This is the central gap between marketing and
substance in most "quantum-ready" blockchain claims: readiness at the ledger layer is
not the same as readiness across an application stack.

This is where ICP's architecture presents a genuinely distinctive — if not yet
battle-tested — advantage. Rather than securing only a token ledger, ICP's chain-key
cryptography underpins compute, storage, identity, and inter-canister communication
across the entire network through unified threshold signature schemes (currently
threshold ECDSA and BLS-based Schnorr variants). Critically, protocol upgrades on ICP —
including, in principle, a full replacement of the underlying signature scheme — are
proposed and voted on through the network's on-chain governance system, and once
approved, are applied automatically across the network without forks and with minimal
downtime, with the full state of all applications preserved. This stands in sharp
contrast to the traditional web's fragmented migration path, and even to most other
blockchains, where a cryptographic primitive change typically requires independent
coordination among wallets, validators, and applications, often via contentious hard
forks.

It is important to be precise about the limits of this advantage. ICP's current
signature schemes (threshold ECDSA and BLS) are themselves built on elliptic-curve
mathematics and are not inherently quantum-resistant — the network does not have a
documented head start on the underlying cryptography itself. Its advantage, rather, is
structural: a credible, tested mechanism for coordinating a network-wide cryptographic
upgrade without fragmenting the ecosystem. That mechanism has been exercised for
routine protocol upgrades, but never yet for a change as fundamental as replacing the
core signature primitive across every subnet — meaning this remains a strong design
pattern on paper rather than a proven one under real quantum pressure.

CONCLUSION

The current web's security model rests substantially on legal promises and contractual
trust — a vendor's word that it will not misuse data, a jurisdiction's law that may or
may not survive a foreign legal challenge. Rising cloud breaches, sovereignty
legislation, and the slow, uneven crawl toward post-quantum migration all point toward
the same underlying weakness: coordination among many independent, self-interested
parties is hard, slow, and prone to failure at the weakest link.

The Internet Computer's bet is that a system where trust is enforced by protocol and
governance — rather than by contract, law, or goodwill — is better positioned to
respond quickly and uniformly to both today's threats and tomorrow's. Its passwordless
identity system already addresses the leading real-world cause of breaches. Its
sovereign cloud engines address the jurisdictional gap that hyperscaler "sovereign"
offerings have struggled to close credibly. And its unified, network-wide governance
model offers a structurally more coordinated path through a quantum transition than
either the fragmented traditional web or the many blockchains whose "quantum-ready"
claims extend no further than their token ledger.

None of this guarantees ICP's success. Adoption today remains small next to
incumbents, enterprise procurement cycles favor proven, boring infrastructure, and
ICP's most important claims — particularly around coordinated post-quantum migration —
remain architecturally sound but operationally unproven at scale. But among projects
attempting to rethink the web's cryptographic foundations, ICP is one of the few
building toward the full scope of the problem, rather than a single narrow slice of it.

text:
I ru|ned my ex-boyfriend’s l!fe 20+ years ago and I just made sure it stayed ruined

When I was in college in the 90s, I met “Jake” (then M23) through mutual friends.  He had already graduated and was planning to move to the opposite side of the United States for grad school and I had already been making plans to move with friends only a 90 minute drive away from where he was moving to.  We had so much in common, fell in love and it really seemed like fate, both planning to move 3000 miles and landing so close together.  He had two sisters and a younger brother who were all awesome people and I became instant friends with them as well.  

Because he was in school and I was working, I would usually go to him to hang out on weekends.  He was renting a house with 2 roommates, also in his program.  We were young so money was tight but we had fun, went for taco dates and spent a lot of time at his house where he was breeding and selling small animals.  Jake was an animal sciences PhD student so being around animals was normal and I loved it.  I met and became friends with his advisor’s wife (“Mary, F mid-50s) who worked in administration at the university.  She is a lovely woman and I would often have lunch with her when I went over on weekends.  Jake was a teaching assistant (TA) and I met other people in the program and made friends with them faster than he did.  

After about 2 years of dating, I was at the house one day, laying in bed together, in a state of some undress and he said out of the blue, he was concerned I’d been gaining weight and it made it harder for him to be attracted to me.  No concern about my health, it was all about him finding me unattractive.  I sat up and said, well, then maybe you should make sure there is better food for me to eat than crackers and cheese when I come up on weekends.  Even at 23, I didn’t take that kind of BS.  I had gained MAYBE 10 pounds since meeting him two years earlier and still wore the same size clothes (about a US size 6-8).  I wasn’t going to engage in a fight about it after all, it was his problem, not mine, so I asked him calmly, so what is your solution to this?  He stared at me blankly and said well, I guess that you should try to lose weight and I said, nah, I’m not going to do that so what are YOU going to do about it.  He said, well, I guess nothing, I wanted to let you know how I feel and I said, cool, thank you, put my clothes back on, went to sleep and drove home the next day as usual.  

We keep dating and about 3 months later he called me and said he wanted to break up after close to 3 years.  The reason AND I QUOTE “You don’t know enough about science”.  He felt like he couldn’t have a conversation with me about his work where he didn’t have to use common names for animals instead of scientific ones.  I said, well, that’s bullshit, what’s the real reason.  He said it was the real reason.  He came to see me a month later to return something of mine and I confronted him, demanding the real reason.  He finally admitted he had been seeing one of his undergrad students, let’s call her Meg, a 19 year old.  He was then 26 and her teacher.  I screamed at him to leave, my roommate threated to throw him off our second floor balcony if he didn’t go and he left.  It hit me all at once after he walked out and I went from rage to stunned laughter.  I’d met Meg a few times and at one point, she was at his house for a BBQ and spilled something all over her pants.  Jake asked me if I could loan her some sweats.  I couldn’t because I was a size 8 and she was a size 18.  Nothing wrong with that, AT ALL, but the point is, I realized he made those comments about my weight to try and get me to break up with HIM because he was a coward.  He clearly liked a big gal.  Although, when he’d said those things to me about my weight it was 1am, I lived about 95 miles away and we had just had sex so I don’t know how he thought this would go, even in hindsight, it’s perplexes me.  
Did he think I was going to break up with him and storm off into the night and drive for an hour and a half?    

ANYWAY, I emailed his roommates, it was the early 2000s, it’s how you communicated anything you didn’t want to say on the phone. I wanted to let them know we'd broken up and that they were always lovely to me and thanked them for being friends.  They both admitted they knew about Meg and were the ones to demand that Jake tell me or they would.  That’s when he broke up with me with the lame, you don’t understand science excuse.  One of his roommate, a super nice, super cute guy named “George” offered to help me get a few things still at their house that he had collected for me away from around the house.  He suggested I come up for the weekend, we go out and drink and have a good time, all the things Jake didn’t want to “waste” money on and I said sure!

text:
To offer some clarity - Whether marriage is a vocation in the same sense as the priesthood or consecrated celibacy is the question. The priesthood and celibacy are supernatural vocations requiring a special call and grace from God. Marriage is a natural state of life which all human beings, even those who become priests, are ordered twd by nature, not requiring a special "calling." Thus it is arguably only called a vocation equivocally.

Meanwhile the Church has no tradition of calling the unconsecrated single state a vocation. The single state becomes a vocation in the same sense as priesthood only when one chooses to be celibate deliberately for supernatural reasons. Otherwise, it is just the state of life you are in (which is a "calling" in the sense that we are all "called" to live the duties of our state in life).

I think the idea that being the unconsecrated (or even involuntary) single state is a vocation has been floated because single people feel left out bc they have been told that marriage and priesthood/religious life are vocations and they want a vocation too. We can solve this feeling of exclusion not by inventing some novel single vocation which has no precedent in our spiritual tradition, but by ceasing to call marriage a Vocation and returning to the much clearer traditional language of the different states of life. Married is a state of life, single is a state of life, etc.

text:
After France fell the mood across Germany from Hitler down to the ordinary infantryman - was that the war in the West was essentially finished. 

France was beaten. 

The British Army had left its guns and its tanks and its trucks on the beaches.

What rational Government staring at those facts would keep fighting alone?

Hitler expected London to come to its senses. 

He waited. 

For weeks he delayed any formal move against Britain expecting a signal, a message, a phone-call. 

It never came. 

By mid-July his patience was running out. On the 16th of July 1940, Hitler issued Fuhrer Direktive Nr. 16 - ordering preparations for Operation Sea Lion — The Invasion of Britain. 

Read its opening line and you can hear his confusion; “As England, in spite of the hopelessness of her military position, has so far shown herself unwilling to come to any compromise. I have decided to prepare for and if necessary carry out an invasion of England.” - “…the hopelessness of her military position…”

That was Berlins assessment, they believed Britain was already beaten and simply refused to admit it. 

Three days later Hitler made one more attempt to make the British see reason, and he turned it into a show. 

The Reichstag gathered on the evening of 19th July at the Kroll Opera House, where it had met ever since the Reichstag fire in 1933. Hitler had combined the session with a victory celebration for the conquest of France. Before he had made his offer of peace, he handed out rewards; in a single ceremony he promoted 12 Generals to the Rank of Field Marshal, an enormous batch deliberately handed out all at once. Rundstedt, Bock, Brauchitsch, Keitel, Kesselring, Milch and more. Then he went further, Herman Goering already a Field Marshal was elevated to an entirely new rank invented for him alone Reichsmarschall. Making him nominally the senior officer of the entire armed forces and confirming him as Hitlers chosen successor. Watching from the Diplomatic seats was an American Radio correspondent named William Shirer. He knew Hitlers performance well and he wrote that night that the Hitler that he saw was: “the conqueror, conscious of it” and yet “so wonderful an actor, so magnificent a handler of the German mind.”

Near Shirer sat the Italian Foreign Minister Count Galeazzo Ciano in the grey and black uniforms of the Fascist militia. Every-time Hitler paused for breath Ciano leapt up like a jack-in-the-box to give the Fascist salute, clutching a text of the speech - he probably couldn’t even follow. 

Then Hitler made his appeal. He was careful to frame it not as a plea but as generosity from a position of total strength; “I am not the vanquished begging favours, but the victor speaking in the name of reason…” He said he could see no reason why the war had to go on and then he came to the heart of it, the passage that hung over everything: “A great empire will be destroyed” he said, “an empire that it was never my intention to destroy or even to harm. This struggle, if it continues, can end only with the complete annihilation of one or the other of the two adversaries. Mr Churchill may believe that this will be Germany, I know that it will be Britain.”

That was the choice laid out. Come to terms or be annihilated. He mixed it with the contempt for Churchill personally calling him “an unscrupulous politician who wrecked whole nations” and sneering that when Germany won Churchill would already be safe in Canada, where the money and the children of the war mongers had supposedly been sent. 

To the Diplomats in that hall it sounded dangerous, precisely because it sounded reasonable. 

There were no harsh detailed demands read out, it was vague. 

A broad invitation to be sensible. 

Some foreign observers in the room worried that the British might actually seize on that as an excuse to open talks. 

The German press and radio presented it exactly as intended “a magnanimous offer from a victor to a beaten foe.”

text:
Replies get buried so QT to elaborate: People’s decisions depend on far more than the evidence sadly. You see it in distrust of autonomous vehicles, the appeal of non-GMO labels, discomfort with recycled drinking water, even paying more for familiar branded medicines. Another study doesn’t necessarily change how someone feels.

I think the data center industry underestimates this. People keep sharing charts about water and electricity, sometimes without fully appreciating the assumptions in the studies ourselves, and expecting the public to come around. 

National averages, local water availability, who pays for grid upgrades - all those distinctions matter. Calling opposition propaganda or pointing out factual errors still leaves the work of earning support.

Federal support helps, but many of the decisions that determine whether a project gets built happen at the state and local level. Support in Washington doesn’t guarantee support from the community hosting A facility. Residents need to understand how the development benefits them and have confidence that their concerns will be addressed.

And I say this as someone who spends a lot of time talking through charts professionally, being a self admitted AI bull, and understanding power & water markets at a deep level. I’m a HUGE believer in AI reducing costs, democratizing intelligence, and being a massive boon to the economy and American infrastructure development.  

I think some of the tech cos should put much more effort into delivering and explaining the benefits: local hiring and apprenticeships, contracts for local businesses, funding for schools and community facilities, and clear commitments on infrastructure costs. Be specific about construction jobs versus permanent jobs and substantiate any claims about lower bills.

Offer free AI tools and practical training through schools, libraries and local businesses. Help people use the technology for something they actually care about. Give residents a say in the development and commitments they can hold the developer to. They should be able to experience the benefits of both the technology and the project being built near them

That is what I am saying. We bridged the gap in the past by buying MiGs and stalling the Marut.

​A similar thing is happening now. Everything including servicing schedules and spare parts demands for a fighter jet is planned far in advance. Did we really just realise today that we need to buy a new aircraft? This is all media hype to build pressure on the government to make a quick decision to buy the Su-57 accompanied by news of a "kill switch" in the Rafale and claims that the Rafale scored 8–0 against Chinese aircraft in a recent exercise in Egypt. These are just paid algorithms used by foreign sellers because India is a massive market.

​Why is this happening right now just before the BRICS summit? Why all the sudden news about Russia being such a great friend who just wants to sell the Su-57 yet refuses to offer 100% Transfer of Technology (ToT) on engine tech or lease the Su-57 to us until we build the AMCA?

​Why not allocate permanent funds for the next 30 years for the AMCA and buy the Su-57 only with the remaining funds? Alternatively we should take it on lease. If Russia wants to sell it .... it should come with 100% ToT on engine design and technology.

​Your simple phrase "bridging the gap" is not that simple.

​It involves buying an aircraft that:

​Is inferior to an adversary's aircraft.

​Is not battle tested. Fighting with Ukraine but not utilising Su-57 to its capability why? Butvtelling the world that its 5th Gen & Stealth.

​Does not come with 100% ToT on engine technology and design. Manufacturing in India is not ToT. Many people get confused with it.

​Will most likely stall our own AMCA project because funds will be consumed by the foreign purchase.

​Think about it this way: if you do not have a permanent house what do you do? You live on rent. That is what I am saying. A fighter jet is like a house that you will depend on for 30 years. If people say "Buy the Su-57 to fill the gap," remember that a fighter jet is not a potato it comes with massive long term dependencies of spares, rotables, lubes, infra, skill manpower, training simulators etc.

​Things taken as stop gap measures should be on rent or lease. You are building your own dream house (the AMCA). Until it is ready live on rent. Do not buy another permanent house paying heavy taxes on buying and selling when your ultimate aim is to build your own house. Buying and living in someone else's house will destroy the dream of building your own because capital is limited.

​What purpose is the Su-57 actually solving?
Is it truly a stop-gap measure?

Just because there is a gap i should have something ... is an incorrect approach to a problem. Fill the gap with other defensive advance denial measures. Have a strong Air Defence which will assist not in Countering Aircrafts but also drones, missiles, loitering munitions etc. Which will be used for 30 years plus, which will make Indian Sky secure. Make strong allies like Israel has US backup always. South Korea has US backup. Europe has NATO with Article 5 to defend so Europe believe in resource pulling of all the NATO countries. N korea has a strong posture and doctrine. China is using the Ocean policies in south China sea to bend the rules. What about diplomatic solutions?
(100 Su57 vs 500 J20) this is a very ineffective basic solution which a school kid can think of. Unke pass kitna mere pass kitna. So a kids thinking is answered in a kids way only unke pass 600+ nukes apne pass 190 nukes only.

A mature person will not coubter fighter woth fighter but will pull in all ways and means to counter.

​If it is a stop-gap, why are we buying it permanently? If the AMCA is ready in 10, 15 or 20 years, are we going to throw these Su-57s away? No, we will still be maintaining and flying them, and we will use high sounding intellectual vocabulary to call them "force multipliers" and vital assets for securing our horizons.

text:
Here is an updated version of a column I wrote ten years ago:

Public Safety and the Mass Incarceration Myth, Revisited
By Michael P. Tremoglie

Ten years ago I argued that "mass incarceration" was a myth manufactured by activists who compared America's prison population to other nations without ever answering the obvious question: what rate of incarceration would satisfy them? A decade later, the well-funded machinery behind that argument — the chorus of foundation-backed advocacy shops — has only grown larger, and its conclusions have hardened. 

Some now claims flatly that increased incarceration has a "marginal-to-zero" effect on crime. Others laughably attribute nearly all of the crime decline since the 1990s to demographics, wages, and policing — not prison. These organizations’ mission is decarceration including publishing research designed to support it.

Another body of research, less quoted by editorial boards, says something very different. The simplest argument for incarceration has nothing to do with deterrence or rehabilitation — it's arithmetic. A person in prison cannot commit a crime against someone outside its walls. 

Analysts at the Manhattan Institute have found that incapacitating a single high-rate offender can prevent an estimated 9.4 serious felonies. That is not a marginal effect. Multiply that figure across the population of repeat, high-frequency offenders who make up a disproportionate share of American prison populations, and the "zero effect" claim starts to look less like a finding and more like an artifact of how the advocacy studies are constructed.

Manhattan Institute researchers have also pointed out a basic flaw in how reform groups measure recidivism: a released prisoner who is not rearrested within three years is not the same as a released prisoner who committed no further crimes. Most offenses go unreported and undetected in the first place. A "clean" three-year recidivism statistic tells you about the criminal justice system's ability to catch people, not about whether crime actually stopped.

For years, activists and progressive prosecutors — Philadelphia's Larry Krasner among the most vocal — have insisted that shorter sentences do not produce more crime. He is leaning on tendentious academic literature claiming length of incarceration has little effect on reoffending. 
But a federal sentencing commission review found the opposite: much of that academic literature suffered from serious methodological flaws, including sample sizes too small to support its sweeping conclusions. 

When researchers reassessed the data, they found that longer sentences were associated with meaningfully lower reoffending. Deterrence, it turns out, depends on certainty, swiftness, and severity working together — not severity alone, but not none of it either.

The real world is not cooperating with the reform narrative. Advocacy groups love to point to states that cut both incarceration and crime simultaneously as proof that decarceration is safe. But the same states offer a less convenient story when crime rises. Louisiana cut its prison population sharply over the last decade — and then, facing a spike in homicides in several of its cities, its own legislature reversed course in 2024, lengthening sentences and curbing parole. If decarceration so reliably delivered public safety, the state's own elected officials would not have felt compelled to reverse it.

Meanwhile, prison populations have grown again nationally since 2022, in 39 states, as crime has fallen to historic lows — a pattern reform groups laughably treat as a warning sign of "backsliding" rather than as evidence that their causal story was incorrect. The point is falling crime is directly related to rising incarceration. The burden of proof for dismantling a system falls on those proposing to dismantle it, not on those urging caution.

I am a constituent in Hazen and I am writing with one specific, no-cost request and a plan behind it.

THE REQUEST

Ask the Treasury Department, by letter or report language, to publish a daily cryptographic hash of the Daily Treasury Statement, every debt-auction result, and every GENIUS Act stablecoin reserve attestation to a public blockchain. Cost: a few dollars a day. No money moves on chain. Nothing changes about how Treasury operates. WHY IT MATTERS

Every budget rule Congress has ever passed failed because the auditors could be outrun. Once the books are anchored where no agency controls them, a future Congress cannot hide a deficit in a footnote, and open-source audit tools run by universities, newsrooms, and citizens can reconcile obligations against outlays in hours instead of the eighteen months a GAO report takes. The audit becomes the enforcement.

THE PLAN IT UNLOCKS

Proof of Books is step one of five. Each step rests on the GENIUS Act, the CLARITY framework, or authority Treasury already has. None needs a new agency.

1. Proof of Books. Anchor every federal ledger to Bitcoin. Bitcoin is the ledger, never the unit of account. The dollar is not pegged to anything.

2. The Dollar Rail. Offer every federal payment, including tax refunds, Social Security, veterans' benefits, and USDA program payments, as an opt-in GENIUS-licensed digital dollar on a public payment network. Those networks already clear hundreds of billions of dollars a month at a fraction of a cent per transaction, in under a second, around the clock. Banks stay in the loop as issuers and custodians. The bridge between the audit chain and the payment chain carries proofs only, never funds, which closes the door that the largest crypto thefts walked through.

3. The Flywheel. Under GENIUS, every digital dollar is backed by a Treasury bill. Every phone on earth holding digital dollars is a bond buyer. We do not fix a $40 trillion debt by forgiving it, which would default on Social Security, pensions, and the very reserves behind digital dollars. We fix it by turning worldwide demand for dollars into demand for Treasuries at the cheapest end of the curve, netting out the roughly $4 trillion the Federal Reserve holds when its balance sheet transfers to Treasury, and offering voluntary exchange into 50 and 100 year bonds so the interest bill becomes fixed instead of refinanced every few years.

4. Strand the Fed. Do not abolish it first; that invites a panic. Move payments and settlement to the public rail, pre-fund an emergency liquidity facility at Treasury and publish it on chain, then replace the rate committee with a published rule anchored on the same ledger. By then the Federal Reserve is a formality and reform is housekeeping.

5. The Restart Bill. Write a primary-balance rule into law, enforced by automatic sequestration that reads the same anchored ledger the public reads. Pair it with programmable federal payments that make farm and industrial policy precise: a crop program payment settled the day the claim clears, a manufacturing credit that lands with the invoice, a Made in USA attestation a buyer can verify.

WHAT IS IN IT FOR THE FIRST DISTRICT

Our farmers wait weeks for USDA disbursements that could clear in seconds. Our merchants hand 2 to 3 percent of every sale to card networks; public rails settle for a fraction of a cent and that money stays in Arkansas. Our community banks become issuers in this system, not casualties of it. And through your seat on the Agriculture Committee, the two networks in this plan are digital commodities within your jurisdiction under CLARITY.

GUARDRAILS

Physical cash stays legal tender. Many licensed issuers, never one. A statutory privacy floor for small payments. A second rail and offline fallback from day one. The public debt stays valid; Section 4 of the 14th Amendment forbids anything else.

BAZAAR JEWELRY: You mentioned that you love cooking. Is there a Korean dish you’re confident in that you’d like to recommend to your Chinese fans? Conversely, is there a Chinese dish you’d like to try making yourself?
Eunseok: I’d like to recommend dishes I love, like stir fried pork or Andong-style braised chicken. Just pairing them with a bowl of warm white rice makes for a simple yet hearty and satisfying meal. As you eat, you’ll probably find yourself thinking, “Ah, today was a good day.”
The Chinese dish I’d like to try making myself is Mapo Tofu. The tofu looks soft and tender, so you’d think it would crumble easily, but when you actually see it, it’s firmer than you’d expect.

BAZAAR JEWELRY: Have you added anything new to your room recently? What kind of “new changes” in your life can we glimpse through that?
Eunseok: I haven’t bought anything new recently. Instead, I bought a new pair of contact lenses, and I’d like to try them out when I get the chance. I also bought a few sets of workout clothes that wick away sweat well and are breathable. I like working out it helps me clear my mind and manage my emotions.

BAZAAR JEWELRY: There are both outgoing and quiet members on the team. As someone who’s “on the quiet side,” do you envy the members’ outgoing personalities? Or do you think being quiet is also an advantage?
Eunseok: I think both personalities have their pros and cons. I don’t dislike my personality as it is. In fact, I think it’s nice to be this way.
Of course, being outgoing and cheerful has the advantage of allowing you to bond with others quickly. In a profession like ours, where we frequently appear in public, I think that kind of personality might be a bit more advantageous.

BAZAAR JEWELRY: “The End of the Day” is a ballad that conveys gratitude to the fans. Given that you’re usually an introvert, which line of this song do you think best expresses what you want to convey to your fans?
Eunseok: There’s a line that goes, “Every day when the sun goes down, I’ll definitely hold you close.” I think this line is the heart of the song.
It’s not when we’re meeting up or cheering each other on—it’s the moment the day ends. After the stage lights go out and all the commotion dies down, that’s the time when people are most exhausted yet most honest. I think the lyrics capture that feeling.
Through this song, I also want to offer a little comfort to Briize, who’s been running around all day and is exhausted. I hope everyone wraps up their day well and gets some rest.

BAZAAR JEWELRY: After wrapping up a full day of magazine photo shoots and interviews, what would you like to do to spend some “me time” with “The End of the Day”?
Eunseok: For me, healing and relaxation don’t have to involve anything complicated. I go home, drink some banana milk, play video games, or get a good night’s sleep. I feel like those simple, comfortable things are what really help me unwind.

text:
The Fiscal Context

The United States entered this debate with a budget deficit projected at $1.853 trillion** for fiscal 2026—about **5.8% of GDP**—according to the Congressional Budget Office's February forecast . The CBO projects the deficit-to-GDP ratio will average **6.1%** over the next decade, reaching **6.7%** by 2036 . Publicly held debt stands at **101% of GDP** in 2026 and is projected to reach **120%** by 2036, surpassing the post-World War II record of 106% . Total national debt crossed **$40 trillion in August 2026, representing 126% of GDP—higher than Germany, the UK, Canada, or France .

The Interest Cost Trap

The most mechanically corrosive element of the fiscal picture is interest. Net interest costs on the federal debt are projected to **more than double to $2 trillion by fiscal 2035**, from $970 billion in fiscal 2025 . These costs now exceed national defense spending and rank as the second-largest federal expenditure. The "snowball" effect—where the effective interest rate on debt approaches or exceeds nominal GDP growth—means the debt ratio can climb even without new borrowing . A $1.2 trillion one-time transfer would require additional borrowing at a moment when the cost of servicing existing debt is already compounding faster than the economy is growing.

The Inflation Risk

Economists have been nearly unanimous in warning that a payment of this scale would fuel inflation. Brian Bethune, an economics professor at Boston College, put it bluntly: "This makes no economic sense" . Heather Long of Navy Federal Credit Union noted that while Americans "would love to receive a $5,000 check," it offers only "short-term gain" followed by "a lot of long-term pain"—higher inflation and higher borrowing costs for homes, cars, and credit cards . The St. Louis Fed estimated that pandemic-era fiscal stimulus added approximately **2.6 percentage points** to inflation . With the Iran war already pushing oil above $100 per barrel, adding demand-side stimulus into a supply-constrained economy would intensify price pressures rather than relieve them .

The Political Reality

House Speaker Mike Johnson immediately clarified that the payment "must be approved by Congress," adding that "the hard part is the details—we have to figure everything out" . The proposal has no legislative vehicle, no eligibility criteria, no funding source, and no timeline . Trump has made similar promises before—a $2,000 "tariff dividend" and a $5,000 "DOGE dividend"—neither of which materialized . The difference now is that the promise is explicitly tied to an electoral outcome.

The Framing

The proposal emerges as Republican midterm prospects face headwinds. A Pew Research survey in July found only 24% of Americans rated the economy as "good" or "excellent," and 60% said Trump's economic policies made things worse . In congressional ballot preference, Democrats led 43% to 37% . The $5,000 offer converts complex debates about deficits, inflation, and war costs into a single, direct question: vote Republican, get cash. Whether voters treat it as a credible commitment or a desperate gamble will be determined on November 3.

Traffic through the Strait of Hormuz has plummeted from a pre-war level of 125 vessels daily to single digits.

Iran is redefining the rules of this waterway through the use of “compliance permits” and “restricted navigation zones.”

This is not an isolated incident.

On August 17, about ten Israeli military vehicles entered Abdin and abducted several young men.

On August 19, Israeli forces again bombarded the Wadi area of Abdin.

On September 11, three shells fired from the occupied Golan Heights landed near the village.

Israel is establishing a de facto “security zone” in southern Syria, systematically eroding Syrian sovereignty under the guise of “reconnaissance flights” and “raids.”
